After years of predicting materials in silico, AI materials discovery is entering the physical world. Google DeepMind is building an automated lab in the UK, startups are deploying self-driving facilities, and researchers are developing new interfaces for human-AI collaboration. But a critical question remains: Can AI overcome real-world complexities that simulations miss?
This comprehensive review covers 22 articles published in December 2025, surveying the latest developments in AI-driven materials discovery. The field is maturing beyond computational prediction to automated experimentation, facing real-world validation challenges, and developing new approaches to bridge the gap between algorithm and laboratory.
The Big Story: AI Goes Physical The most significant infrastructure investment in AI materials discovery to date comes from Google DeepMind, which is building its first automated research laboratory for material discovery in the United Kingdom. Scheduled to be operational by 2026 , the facility will combine Gemini AI with advanced robotics to synthesize and analyze hundreds of material samples daily targeting applications like superconductors, high-performance batteries, solar cells, chips, and medical imaging.
The lab is part of a broader partnership with the UK government that includes sharing AI models with the UK AI Security Institute and providing British researchers priority access to AI systems. Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind, announced the initiative in December 2025, alongside UK Technology Secretary Liz Kendall. Google has separately committed £5 billion ($6.3 billion) to data-center and operational investments in the UK over the next two years.
This UK facility is one component of a larger strategy. Google DeepMind is also partnering with the U.S. Department of Energy as part of the White House’s Genesis Mission a national effort to use AI to accelerate scientific research. Through this partnership, Google will provide all 17 DOE National Laboratories with access to its frontier AI models and tools, starting with the AI co-scientist built on Gemini. The collaboration aims to accelerate breakthroughs in energy, materials discovery, and national security, with an accelerated access program expanding to National Laboratories in early 2026 .
Despite these major infrastructure investments, the field has yet to produce a major commercial breakthrough. As MIT Technology Review notes in its analysis , AI-driven materials discovery is moving from computational simulation to real-world experimentation, but the critical bottleneck remains physically making and testing predicted compounds. The typical timeline to develop and manufacture a new material still spans 20 years and no AI-discovered material has yet achieved commercial scale.
Bridging the Prediction-Reality Gap The fundamental challenge in AI materials discovery is no longer prediction, it is physical synthesis and testing. The field is developing multiple approaches to bridge this gap.
Startup Approaches Venture-backed startups are building autonomous labs where AI agents design and run experiments to synthesize and optimize new materials. Lila Sciences, co-founded by Rafael Gómez-Bombarelli (MIT professor of materials science) with chief autonomous science officer John Gregoire, has raised hundreds of millions of dollars to pursue this approach. Periodic Labs, co-founded by physicist Ekin Dogus Cubuk and Liam Fedus (co-creator of ChatGPT), is building similar facilities focused on automated experimentation.
These startups aim to drastically shorten the decades-long development timeline for new materials needed for batteries, carbon capture, and next-generation computing. Their autonomous labs use techniques like sputtering for materials deposition, with AI agents conducting experiments at scales impractical for human researchers.
Human-in-the-Loop Systems Rather than full automation, some researchers are finding success with collaborative human-AI frameworks. Scientists from Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering developed an AI advisor model that enables shared control in self-driving labs. Applied to electronic materials, specifically mixed ion-electron conducting polymers (MIECPs), the system achieved a 150% performance improvement over previous cutting-edge techniques.
The research, published in Nature Chemical Engineering, introduces an adaptive AI decision interface for autonomous experimentation that enables real-time human-AI collaboration. The platform successfully optimized conducting polymers in just 64 autonomous trials , achieving a mixed-conducting figure of merit (\(\mu C^*\)) ranging from 166 to 1,275 F cm\(^{-1}\) V\(^{-1}\) s\(^{-1}\) . The work also uncovered a previously unknown polymer polymorph , demonstrating the platform’s potential for accelerated materials discovery through adaptive experimentation that combines AI data analysis with human decision-making.
Concrete Discoveries While much of the focus is on methodology, AI is also producing tangible materials discoveries.
Magnetic Sensors Researchers at the National Institute for Materials Science (NIMS) developed a high-throughput experimental method that measures anomalous Hall resistivity 30 times faster than conventional techniques. Combining this method with machine learning, they discovered a new ternary magnetic sensor material (Fe-Ir-Pt) with a record-high anomalous Hall resistivity of 6.5 \(\mu\Omega \cdot cm\) significantly exceeding the previous maximum of 5.25 \(\mu\Omega \cdot cm\) in Fe-X binary systems.
The new method reduces evaluation time per composition to 0.2 hours (12 minutes) , enabling rapid screening of compositional gradient thin films. This data-driven pipeline accelerates the search for sensitive magnetic sensor materials crucial for next-generation hard disk drives, published in npj Computational Materials.
Superconductors Tohoku University and Fujitsu Limited used the Fujitsu Kozuchi AI platform to analyze the superconductivity mechanism of a kagome superconducting material, cesium vanadium antimonide (CsV\(_3\)Sb\(_5\)). Their new discovery intelligence technique compressed causal graphs derived from complex experimental data to 1/20th of their original size , enabling efficient identification of the material’s electron interactions.
The research leverages data from the NanoTerasu Synchrotron Light Source (operational since April 2024) and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). Fujitsu plans to begin offering a trial environment for the discovery intelligence technology in March 2026 , following the 2022 establishment of the Fujitsu x Tohoku University Discovery Intelligence Laboratory.
LLM-Powered Discovery Researchers at the University of Tokyo developed MatAgent, an AI framework using large language models for autonomous and explainable materials discovery. The system reasons step-by-step in natural language , explains its decisions, and incorporates user constraints to efficiently search for new inorganic materials. Published in Cell Reports Physical Science, the approach aims to accelerate discovery of materials for catalysis, energy storage, and semiconductors by making AI-driven discovery more transparent and explainable.
Other Discoveries Topological materials: Researchers from the University of Alabama at Birmingham and Shenzhen University developed a quantum-inspired chemical rule using a hybrid quantum-classical artificial neural network to predict topological materials from chemical composition, achieving 84.7% prediction accuracy and successfully identifying new topological compounds.
Ultralow thermal conductivity: A study in Nature Communications introduced a universal descriptor for thermal conductivity based on atomic number and sound velocity, enabling fast screening of materials. Using high-throughput workflows and machine learning, researchers identified candidates from over 25,000 materials and experimentally validated record-low thermal conductivity in CsAg\(_2\)I\(_3\).
The Reality Check As the field scales up, researchers are identifying specific technical limitations that AI-based materials prediction must overcome.
The Crystallographic Disorder Problem An international study led by the University of Bayreuth, Fritz Haber Institute, and Imperial College London reveals that AI and computer simulations often make significant errors in predicting material properties because they ignore crystallographic disorder a common feature in real-world crystals. The researchers developed a machine-learning tool to detect disordered materials and found that in one database, over 80% of AI-predicted promising materials were likely affected by disorder that simulations missed.
The tool, published in Advanced Materials, addresses substitutional disorder a phenomenon where multiple elements randomly occupy crystallographic sites. Prof. Dr. Johannes T. Margraf (University of Bayreuth) and first author Konstantin Jakob (Fritz Haber Institute) present the detection tool as a way to improve reliability and efficiency of computer-assisted material discovery, preventing costly experimental failures based on flawed predictions.
Acknowledging Limitations MIT Technology Review examines the gap between promise and reality , noting that while Google’s DeepMind has predicted millions of new materials, only hundreds have actually been made in the lab . The publication characterizes the field as still in early stages and prone to hype, with significant challenges in translating AI predictions into novel, useful, and physically viable materials.
Similarly, Semiconductor Engineering reviews the benefits and limits of machine learning for materials discovery. While ML tools enable a 100-fold reduction in candidates for synthesis, the analysis emphasizes that these tools rely heavily on human expertise for data preparation, validation, and interpretation to overcome limitations like selection bias and model explainability. Case studies from IBM, Microsoft Research, and Samsung demonstrate that ML integration with human judgment is essential for reliable outcomes.
Methodological Advances Beyond applications, researchers are developing new computational and experimental frameworks for AI-accelerated materials science.
Computational Methods A review in Nature Computational Materials discusses how machine learning and quantum computing can accelerate discovery of high-entropy materials for energy applications like batteries and supercapacitors. The work focuses on overcoming data and modeling obstacles to predict material properties before physical synthesis, highlighting the potential of high-entropy MXenes to overcome limitations of conventional battery materials.
Researchers from the University of Manchester are using AI to accelerate quantum materials discovery, with an AI system that “learns to think like a physicist” to predict promising materials and guide their fabrication. Led by Dr. Qian Yang (Royal Society University Research Fellow at the National Graphene Institute), the work aims to underpin breakthroughs in lossless superconductors and clean energy catalysts.
Experimental Integration A study in Nature Computational Materials presents an Active Learning loop implementation in pyiron for experimental materials characterization, combining experimental and simulated data. The approach uses prior knowledge from density functional theory simulations and text mining to accelerate characterization, drawing inspiration from high-throughput simulation workflows to bridge computation and experiment.
Researchers propose a framework for networking autonomous material exploration systems using transfer learning to share knowledge and improve discovery efficiency. Demonstrated with three distinct systems targeting different material properties, the approach uses ensemble neural networks and Bayesian optimization to enable large-scale autonomous networks that could accelerate material development through knowledge exchange.
Quantum Applications A research team including scientists from General Motors demonstrates that quantum algorithms can accurately simulate transition metal oxides used in automotive catalysts. Their resource estimation shows simulating a key catalyst fragment to chemical accuracy could require 300 to 10 million physical qubits , a scale projected for future hardware. Led by Yuntao Gu, Louis Hector, Jr, and Paolo Giusto from GM, the work validates applying quantum computing to real-world materials science and provides a roadmap for near-term simulations of catalytic materials.
Funding and Ecosystem Startup activity continues in the materials discovery space. Novyte Materials raised INR 4.15 crore (approximately $50,000) in a pre-seed round led by Theia Ventures. The startup uses generative AI and physics-based simulations to compress R&D timelines by 10 times and reduce early-stage physical testing costs by 90% . The funding represents Theia Ventures’ fourth investment from its new fund, which announced its first close in October 2025.
While modest compared to the hundreds of millions raised by Lila Sciences, the investment shows continued startup activity in AI-driven materials discovery despite the field’s lack of commercial breakthroughs.
Looking Ahead The developments of December 2025 reveal a field in transition. Google DeepMind’s automated lab represents a major bet that physical experimentation at scale is the path forward. The human-AI collaboration work suggests pure automation isn’t the only answer hybrid approaches that combine AI’s analytical capabilities with human judgment may prove more effective. The crystallographic disorder study reveals specific, addressable technical challenges that must be overcome for AI predictions to translate reliably to real materials.
The lack of commercial breakthroughs, as noted by MIT Technology Review, suggests the field is still in early days despite the hype and investment. AI may accelerate discovery from decades to years, not months. The realistic timeline for AI-discovered materials to reach commercial application remains measured in years, not months.
Approach Key Example Status Fully Automated Labs Google DeepMind UK facility Opening 2026 Human-AI Collaboration AI advisor at Argonne 150% performance gain demonstrated Startup Labs Lila Sciences, Periodic Labs Early stage, no major breakthroughs As 2026 approaches, the key question for the field is: Will physical validation match the computational promise? The Google DeepMind lab, scheduled to open next year, will be a critical test case. Success would validate the large-scale investment in automated experimentation. Continued challenges would reinforce the value of hybrid human-AI approaches and highlight the need for continued fundamental research into the complexities of real-world materials.
The field is growing up identifying specific problems like crystallographic disorder, developing concrete solutions like disorder-detection ML tools, and building infrastructure like the UK automated lab. This maturation from hype to measured progress may be the most important development of all.
title: AI Materials Discovery Moves Beyond Simulation

This comprehensive review covers 65 articles published during December 2025, surveying the latest developments in quantum computing. As the field matures from hype toward measurable progress, researchers proposed standardized KPIs to evaluate quantum systems, silicon-based chips demonstrated record fidelities, and error correction crossed new thresholds globally.
The Big Story: Quantum Computing Seeks Standard Metrics As quantum computing matures, the field is grappling with a fundamental problem: how to objectively measure progress. In December, researchers proposed key performance indicators (KPIs) to standardize the evaluation of quantum systems, aiming to distinguish genuine breakthroughs from spurious claims. The effort, documented in a 2025 preprint by Lall et al., seeks to provide comparable metrics across different hardware platforms, algorithms, and evaluation methods.
The push for standardization comes as the field grapples with what metrics actually matter. Research published in Nature Communications and elsewhere has shown that stabilizer metrics may only provide an upper bound on quantum performance, not a complete picture of system capability. Meanwhile, researchers have mapped how errors evolve over time in quantum memory systems, providing better context for what reliability claims mean in practice.
Concrete verification methods are also emerging. Scientists at Swinburne University developed techniques to verify the accuracy of Gaussian Boson Sampler (GBS) devices, quickly identifying errors in experiments that would take thousands of years to simulate classically. The method can detect deviations from expected results, a critical capability as quantum systems grow too complex for classical verification.
This focus on measurement reflects a broader shift in the field. As McKinsey noted in a December analysis , quantum leaders and investors are increasingly prioritizing quantum error correction as the critical path to utility, with investment in quantum startups surging 50% in 2024.
Error Correction Breakthroughs Microwave Control Advances Chinese researchers achieved a significant milestone in December, demonstrating fault-tolerant quantum error correction using an all-microwave method on a 107-qubit processor. This marks the first time a group outside the US has crossed this key reliability threshold. The team, led by Pan Jianwei from the University of Science and Technology of China, achieved an error-suppression factor of 1.4 with a distance-7 surface-code logical qubit—a scale comparable to Google’s recent advances.
The microwave-based approach offers a practical advantage: it suppresses leakage errors without requiring extra hardware, potentially easing scaling bottlenecks. As reported in Physical Review Letters , the method tackles qubit drift and error propagation more efficiently than hardware-intensive approaches.
Complementary research from the same team demonstrated a new method to fix leakage errors using targeted microwave pulses . Tested on a 97-qubit processor, the technique suppressed leakage errors over 70 times more effectively than running without suppression. Critically, the system became more reliable as more qubits were added—a key requirement for scalable quantum computing.
Hardware Solutions European researchers achieved a breakthrough in superconducting qubit control, developing analytical formulas called R1D and R2D that achieve gate fidelities of 99.999% for rapid X-gate rotations. The work from Forschungszentrum Jülich, University of Cologne, and RWTH Aachen University addresses limitations in qubit control under strong driving, providing a blueprint for more reliable quantum processors.
On the decoding side, Riverlane published a peer-reviewed paper in Nature Communications detailing its Local Clustering Decoder (LCD), a hardware decoder that achieves real-time quantum error correction for the surface code. The decoder breaks the traditional trade-off between speed and accuracy, performing one round in under a microsecond and adapting to changing noise conditions. It forms the core of Riverlane’s Deltaflow stack and has been deployed on systems from partners including Infleqtion and Rigetti Computing.
Silicon Chips Show Record Fidelities Silicon Quantum Computing (SQC) published breakthrough results in Nature in December, demonstrating an 11-qubit quantum processor in silicon that achieves fidelity rates between 99.5% and 99.99% . The processor uses a novel “14/15” architecture that places phosphorus atoms in silicon with atomic precision, achieving feature sizes of just 0.13 nanometers.
The significance of this work goes beyond the numbers. As SQC’s research shows, their silicon-based processor scales without losing fidelity —qubit quality actually improves as qubit count increases, contrary to typical quantum systems. The architecture demonstrates atomic, silicon-based quantum computing across separate clusters for the first time, with multi-register linkages maintaining fidelities above fault-tolerance benchmarks.
This modular approach addresses what SQC calls the key quantum scaling problem : how to connect qubit registers while preserving high gate fidelities. The company’s proprietary atomic-scale manufacturing process, developed over 25 years, allows it to produce its own quantum chips with 0.13 nanometer precision.
On the commercialization front, SEALSQ announced a CMOS-compatible roadmap targeting quantum processor production from 2026 to 2030, positioning silicon-based approaches as a potentially manufacturable path to scale.
Capital Moves: Quantum Art $100M, Government Investments Private Funding Quantum Art closed a $100 million Series A funding round to scale its multi-core trapped-ion quantum computers, bringing total funding to $124 million. The round, one of the largest for trapped-ion systems, will accelerate development of the company’s 1,000-qubit Perspective system and prototyping of a third-generation architecture targeting thousands of qubits. The company also demonstrated a 200-ion chain and collaborations with NVIDIA and Ayalon Highways.
Nu Quantum raised $60 million in Series A funding , the largest financing round for quantum computer networking. The Cambridge-based company is developing quantum networking technology to enable distributed quantum computing.
QubitSolve secured a $1.2 million NSF SBIR Phase II grant to accelerate development of its quantum computational fluid dynamics (CFD) software. The Morgantown-based startup is transitioning from a 2D prototype to a 3D minimum viable product, with commercial release targeted for late 2027.
Government Investment Canada launched the Canadian Quantum Champions Program, allocating up to $92 million in initial public funding to four domestic quantum firms—Anyon Systems, Nord Quantique, Photonic, and Xanadu Quantum Technologies. This Phase 1 initiative is part of a broader $334.3 million investment from Budget 2025 aimed at strengthening Canada’s quantum ecosystem and developing fault-tolerant quantum computers.
The Oak Ridge Quantum Science Center secured $125 million in DOE funding for its 2025-2030 program, focusing on quantum materials research and joined-up, multidisciplinary approaches to quantum challenges.
Fujitsu announced a $100,000 quantum simulator challenge , inviting researchers to tackle real-world problems using its 40-qubit quantum simulator.
Company Amount Type Focus Quantum Art $100M Series A Trapped-ion systems Nu Quantum $60M Series A Quantum networking Canada Champions $92M Government 4 domestic firms Oak Ridge QSC $125M DOE funding 2025-30 program Global Quantum Deployments Accelerate Europe Spain’s CESGA selected IQM Quantum Computers and Telefónica to deploy two on-premises quantum computers: a 54-qubit IQM Radiance system and a 5-qubit IQM Spark for education. Scheduled for delivery by June 2026, this marks Spain’s first quantum-HPC integration and IQM’s first installation in the country.
In Germany, Universal Quantum and Atlas Copco partnered to co-develop industrial-grade vacuum systems for scalable trapped-ion quantum computers. The collaboration aims to transition vacuum technology from laboratory tools to integrated solutions for modular quantum architectures.
FullStaQD announced a new quantum software stack to optimize quantum application development, part of broader European efforts to build complete quantum computing ecosystems.
Qilimanjaro and Oxigen Data Center partnered on multimodal quantum-HPC integration, enabling hybrid quantum-classical workflows for Spanish researchers.
Asia-Pacific & Middle East Israel’s Quantum Computing Center (IQCC) deployed Qolab’s scalable superconducting qubit device , marking the first installation of the Nobel laureate-founded company’s hardware outside its US lab. The device uses Quantum Machines’ control technology and will be available via cloud access.
Chile launched a National Quantum Strategy 2025-2035 , prioritizing sovereign capabilities in quantum computing, sensing, and communications. The strategy aims to transition Chile to a knowledge-based economy with applications in mining, energy, and telecommunications.
India’s Andhra Pradesh unveiled a Quantum Vision plan to establish Amaravati as a global quantum computing hub among the world’s top five. The initiative targets local quantum computer production within two years and includes a Rs 100-crore (approximately $12 million) Nobel Prize award for quantum research.
In Singapore, Keysight Technologies entered a five-year collaboration with A*STAR, NUS, and NTU to co-develop scalable qubit control architectures, integrating digital control systems with novel processor architectures.
Xanadu expanded its partnership with A*STAR to advance photonic quantum computing, strengthening Singapore’s position in the quantum landscape.
The UK’s National Quantum Computing Centre partnered with Google to give UK researchers access to Google’s advanced Willow quantum chip through an open competition, aiming to uncover new real-world applications in chemistry and medicine.
Location System Qubits Timeline Partner Spain (CESGA) IQM Radiance 54 By June 2026 IQM, Telefónica Israel (IQCC) Qolab Scalable Deployed Qolab, Quantum Machines Chile National Strategy N/A 2025-2035 Government-led Research Roundup: Optical Chips, Algorithms, and Applications Optical Advances Researchers developed a tiny optical phase modulator nearly 100 times smaller than a human hair that uses 80 times less microwave power than commercial modulators. The device, from University of Colorado at Boulder and Sandia National Laboratories, uses microwave-frequency vibrations to manipulate laser light and is manufactured using scalable CMOS fabrication. This breakthrough could enable control of thousands or millions of qubits for trapped-ion and trapped-neutral-atom quantum computers.
Multiple publications highlighted the significance of this work. As reported in ScienceDaily , the chip oscillates billions of times per second and is aimed at the critical bottleneck of optical control for scaling quantum computers. Stanford University researchers separately demonstrated room-temperature quantum communication using molybdenum diselenide and silicon nanostructures, potentially enabling low-cost quantum technologies without extreme cooling.
Algorithms & Software Researchers developed CircPack, a framework for parallel execution of quantum circuits on trapped-ion computers that treats circuit scheduling as a packing problem. The framework achieves up to 70.72% higher fidelity, 62.67% better utilization, and 32.80% improved layer reduction compared to existing methods, enhancing quantum cloud computing efficiency.
Nature Communications published research on AI integration into the quantum stack, demonstrating how machine learning can optimize quantum operations.
Neutral-Atom Progress Researchers at Xiangtan University trapped 2,400 Ytterbium-174 atoms in an optical tweezer array with 83.5% loading efficiency, a significant improvement in scalability for quantum computing. The achievement, using optimized laser cooling and real-time feedback, paves the way for larger quantum systems with estimated two-qubit gate fidelities of 99.9%.
Atom Computing developed a method for “qubit recycling” , replenishing atoms from a separate trap to reduce errors and atom loss in neutral-atom quantum computers. Published in Physical Review X, the work enables more complex and longer quantum circuits.
Russian researchers from Lomonosov Moscow State University tested a 72-qubit quantum computer based on neutral rubidium atoms, achieving 94% accuracy in two-qubit operations. The system uses a three-zone architecture for computation, storage, and readout, with plans to reach several hundred high-fidelity qubits by 2030.
Applications Xanadu published a quantum computational framework demonstrating how fault-tolerant quantum computers can model photosensitizers for photodynamic cancer therapy. The research provides resource estimates for utility-scale hardware and projects significant runtime reductions for classical simulation bottlenecks. The announcement coincided with Xanadu’s planned business combination expected to provide approximately $500 million in capital.
Researchers from IBM, RIKEN, Google, and Quantinuum demonstrated progress in applying quantum computers to chemistry problems throughout 2025 . Qunova Computing reported a quantum algorithm achieving 10 times the efficiency of traditional methods for chemistry calculations.
Nature published research on quantum computing methods for materials simulation, expanding the range of applications for near-term quantum hardware.
Networked Systems IonQ published a study finding that linked quantum computers can outperform larger single systems. The research suggests a modular approach to scaling rather than building monolithic processors.
Japan achieved a milestone in remote quantum computing , enabling cloud-based access to quantum systems across geographical distances.
Industry Briefs Amazon reorganized its quantum computing efforts , combining AI, silicon, and quantum computing under a unified structure to streamline development and resource allocation.
Microsoft’s Majorana 1 quantum computer chip continued to generate discussion and controversy . The chip relies on unproven topological qubits based on Majorana zero modes, with some experts remaining unconvinced by the data. Microsoft’s project advanced to the final phase of DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative.
IonQ highlighted the historical significance of Dr. Chris Monroe’s 1995 quantum logic gate , which marked the practical birth of quantum computing. The company, founded in 2015, now targets 80,000 logical qubits by 2030 and recently announced a world-record 99.99% two-qubit gate fidelity.
IBM announced expansion of its Quantum program in Poughkeepsie, New York, planning to build the world’s first large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers by 2033 via its Starling (2029) and Bluejay (2033) projects. The expansion is part of IBM’s broader $1 billion investment in quantum services.
Quantum Computing Inc. agreed to acquire Luminar Semiconductor for $110 million in an all-cash transaction, bringing photonic technologies, patents, and talent to accelerate its quantum systems roadmap.
D-Wave announced it will showcase its quantum computing technology at CES 2026, highlighting real-world customer success stories and applications.
The telecom industry is preparing for quantum computing’s impact by enhancing network security with quantum-safe technologies like post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD). Companies including Orange Business, Telefónica, and Nokia are offering solutions and exploring quantum computing for network optimization.
MOTH, a quantum technology company, announced that quantum computing can overcome classical computing limits in game development, introducing Archaeo, a hardware-agnostic quantum platform for creative workflows, and highlighting Space Moths, a multiplayer game that uses quantum computers to generate levels in real time.
Looking Ahead to 2026 The developments of December 2025 point to a field maturing toward practical applications. Microsoft has introduced a three-level framework for quantum computing progress , with level-two error-corrected machines set for delivery in 2026. These machines, built by Microsoft with Atom Computing and by QuEra, use neutral atoms as qubits for improved scalability and error correction.
The partnership between Microsoft and Atom Computing will deliver the Magne machine with 50 logical qubits and 1,200 physical qubits by the start of 2027. QuEra’s machine at AIST will feature 37 logical qubits across 260 physical qubits. These systems mark the transition from NISQ-era devices to the first generation of error-corrected quantum computers.
McKinsey’s analysis emphasizes that quantum error correction is the priority for capturing value from quantum technologies, which could generate between $0.9 trillion and $2.0 trillion by 2035. The firm notes that quantum start-up investments were 50% higher in 2024 than 2023, with the market projected to reach nearly $100 billion by 2035.
Looking at 2025 investment trends, The Quantum Insider reports a shift away from broad experimentation toward more targeted bets on trapped-ion and photonic hardware architectures, cloud-accessible quantum software platforms, and quantum security technologies. Individual funding rounds for trapped-ion and photonic quantum computer companies reached the $1 billion range.
IBM’s roadmap targets fully error-corrected quantum machines by 2029 , with large-scale systems capable of 1 billion quantum operations by 2029 and 1 billion operations by 2033. The company positions the Hudson Valley as “Quantum Valley,” building on its history of mainframe computing innovation.
As the University of Oxford’s new Quantum Institute Director Ian Walmsley noted , the field is setting the agenda for the next century of quantum science, with deep expertise and cross-disciplinary collaboration accelerating impact across computing, communications, and sensing.
title: Measuring Quantum Progress: Error Correction, Silicon Chips, and the Push for Standardization

content:
The 2022 ChatGPT Moment When ChatGPT was announced at the end of 2022, I spent hours talking to it, genuinely amazed at how it was a step up compared to the previous GPT-3 models (davinci, curie, if those ring a bell). Around that time, I had been on-and-off playing with LangChain to build tool-using agents. While the agents felt unreliable, they made for great demo-ware. The pace of innovation was staggering. The LangChain team shipped new features in a matter of hours, a sign that the AI space was heating up fast.
For the next few weeks, I was playing with ChatGPT almost non-stop, with mixed feelings. Hallucination was real, and it was really hard to get the 3.5-turbo models to follow instructions reliably. It constantly made up wrong citations and could not do simple math. Even GPT-4 could not count the number of letters in a word.
Building Copilot for Chemistry At the time, I was working on Azure Quantum Elements, which aimed to bring together HPC, AI, and quantum computing for scientific discovery. We had data and models for molecules and materials, so it was natural to try LangChain’s ReAct agent for coordinating the execution of those tools. The agent worked well when the problem space and user’s questions matched the narrow fields it was designed for.
Based on the demo’s promise, we realized this seemed to be the future. We rallied a team to intensely work on developing Copilot in Azure Quantum for chemistry and materials. Around the same time, the ChemCrow (Bran et al., 2023) paper came out, and the results gave us a lot of confidence.
We announced Azure Quantum Elements and the Copilot in June 2023 (Zander, 2023). It was a really fun time when a small group of us worked day and night, including weekends for months to make that happen, navigating the responsible AI process along the way. Nobody was asked to work overtime, but everyone was always online to deploy, test, and fix things fast.
Looking back, we had a few good ideas that were probably ahead of their time. We had a rendering window for molecules and calculation results. Later people invented a new term for this UX, namely “Generative UI.” In the scientific field, we deal with big data objects in addition to text responses. Passing large calculation data was nontrivial, and we invented a new way to do that given the limited context of language models.
Workflow vs Agent In an ideal world, I envisioned that the service would evolve into what we now call an “AI Scientist.” The reality is like many early AI services: the churn rate was high. It was reasonably popular for some time, then user engagement dropped and it no longer made sense to maintain. To this date, the only thing I could quickly find was in this blog post (Chen & Almulla, 2023). AI (even with GPT-4, the best model at the time) was still not great at understanding human instructions, and the system was not very reliable, as people reported edge cases all the time. We tried to automate the tests, but the APIs were slow and those are more like regression tests, instead of trying to predict what new queries users may come up with. Again, if we were to build it today, the development of LLM evaluation field and automated red teaming would help us solve some of those.
This made us wonder if a workflow-based system would make more sense. The LangChain blog had a nice analysis on this topic (Chase, 2025).
Obviously, people in the AI space realized this earlier than we did, and LangGraph was developed to address these reliability concerns using more deterministic execution graphs (perhaps also fixing the confusing interface from LangChain). The concept of agentic workflows was later integrated into Microsoft’s Agentic Framework, after a few branding iterations and mergers with other tools like Semantic Kernel, AutoGen, etc. (Microsoft, 2025).
The Reasoning Revolution Beyond the reliability issues, we also realized something deeper was missing. A scientific process (or arguably any complex task) requires more than a chatbot. They require more of “System 2” thinking (slow/deliberate/reflective processes) than “System 1” thinking (fast/automatic/intuitive processes) (Kahneman, 2011).
The famous Chain-of-Thought paper (Wei et al., 2022) was groundbreaking, albeit simple. By eliciting reasoning steps, language models like ChatGPT were able to achieve better results, mimicking how humans work. Then there were several very interesting prompting techniques. Something I recall trying with a colleague was adding “take a deep breath” from DeepMind (Yang et al., 2023). It’s funny, but in some cases it worked.
The o-series reasoning models from OpenAI made a splash. They pioneered test-time compute and extended the chain-of-thought idea by spending more tokens to achieve much better results. This unlocked so many doors and was perhaps a key moment for AI in scientific discovery.
I was switching between ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude around that time. Then Deep Research from both Gemini and ChatGPT really won me over as a user, and Claude was just in its own league for software engineering tasks. I ended up paying for all of them to this day. It seemed inches away to connect deep research with automated software engineering for autonomous research engineering work.
The Rise of AI Scientists and the Return of Agents While many teams were looking into deterministic workflows due to reliability concerns, the rapid improvements in reasoning capabilities quietly made fully autonomous agents viable again. While Microsoft was pitching the concept of “Copilot”, a related concept of “AI (co-)Scientist” took off. It started with Gomes’ team publishing their results on Coscientist in (Boiko et al., 2023). Later, Google shared their AI co-Scientist (Gottweis et al., 2025), and fast forward to recent news where FutureHouse released Kosmos after a few product iterations (Mitchener et al., 2025).
The fundamental idea is surprisingly simple. In some way, it is running reasoning and tool calling in a loop. Lilian Weng’s blog (Weng, 2023) is a great resource on the high-level concepts. But of course, building a reliable one is extremely hard, something we faced every day during the Copilot development.
With frontier AI labs pushing intelligence forward, the distinction between workflows and AI agents becomes blurrier. I personally found, particularly in the last few months, that agentic systems can achieve fairly reliable execution while being more flexible across many tasks. I started to truly feel that we are entering the agentic era from the chatbot generative AI era. Jensen Huang was definitely right on this.
The Copilot for Chemistry initiative was not completely lost. Earlier this year, Microsoft Discovery (Microsoft, 2025) was announced, pushing to build an agentic platform for science. My previous work on AI-accelerated battery electrolyte discovery (Chen et al., 2024) was used as an example of how AI can help accelerate scientific discovery. AI brings unique value to science.
What’s Next? One big trend in 2025 was seeing startups in AI for materials science or physical AI companies with a heavy component in materials raising big funding rounds, again reiterating Jensen’s vision about the future of physical AI. The Genesis Mission executive order (The White House, 2025) pushes the heat to another level. It all makes a lot of sense, as materials and engineering serve as the building blocks for our society. From my past work in this space, it was very clear to me that AI is going to help discover a lot of materials, and it is only a matter of execution, validation, and scale. Perhaps this by itself will be another blog post at a later stage.
The data question is becoming central: the whole internet’s data is somewhat exhausted, so you would need to generate synthetic data or experimental data. Lots of experiments in science, if you capture all the data, can be extremely valuable if one knows how to merge that data with existing data and figure out a path towards scientific superintelligence.
This is likely where quantum computing enters the picture. As I work in the quantum computing industry, I see a natural connection: materials and molecules fundamentally operate on quantum mechanics principles, which classical computers struggle to simulate accurately. Quantum computers could generate training data that captures physics classical systems cannot, potentially unlocking new frontiers for AI in science. 2026 is going to be another exciting year for AI for Science.
What I Learned If I had to summarize what the past few years taught me:
We kept hitting reliability problems, not capability problems. The demos were always impressive, but getting things to work in production was a different story. Users found edge cases we never thought of, and maintenance became a full-time job that few want to take.
The reasoning models (o1, o3) were the unlock. Before that, we were patching unreliable systems with workflows. After that, agents actually started working.
We went from agents to workflows and back to agents. It felt like going in circles, but the second time around, the agents were better. Sometimes you have to retreat before you can advance.
And now everyone is talking about data. The internet is tapped out. Science has data that nobody else has, and that might be the edge. The nice part about science is that you can validate in real world.
Final Words I have long hoped to build an agent that can automate myself. Deep Research was probably the first tool that I felt was powerful enough to replace part of myself for literature review and information gathering. The barrier to entering a new field has never been lower. During the break, I decided to build an agent for writing research review articles for me. The following is a 148-page zero-shot generation (plus answering the clarification questions) of my “literature-reviewer” agent using the prompt “Impacts and potentials of quantum computing for artificial intelligence”.
If you’re curious about how quantum computing can help build better AI, take a look:
Impacts and Potentials of Quantum Computing for Artificial Intelligence: A Comprehensive Review
It is not perfect, but it is a fitting way to close 2025. A year where the tools we dreamed of building finally started building themselves.

title: 2025 Reflection on AI and Agents

content:
This comprehensive review covers 159 articles published in November 2025, surveying the latest developments in AI agents. This month brought a crucial reality check for AI agents. Multiple independent studies revealed agents struggling to work autonomously, Microsoft bet big on “Agent 365” as an operating system for AI agents, and security researchers documented the first cases of malicious agent use. Yet amid the sobering news, real deployments showed tangible results.
The Performance Reality Check The most significant story this month was the mounting evidence that AI agents, as currently built, cannot work independently. A landmark study from Upwork drew from more than 300 real client projects and found that AI agents routinely fail to complete even straightforward professional tasks on their own. The research tested leading models—Gemini 2.5 Pro, OpenAI’s GPT-5, and ClaudeSonnet 4—on actual jobs posted by paying clients.
The results were stark. When working alone, AI agents showed low completion rates across the board. For data science and analytics projects, ClaudeSonnet 4 achieved a 64% completion rate independently but jumped to 93% after receiving feedback from a human expert. In sales and marketing work, Gemini 2.5 Pro’s completion rate rose from 17% independently to 31% with human input . OpenAI’s GPT-5 showed similarly dramatic improvements in engineering tasks, climbing from 30% to 50% completion with human oversight .
When AI agents collaborate with human experts, project completion rates surge by up to 70% . This finding challenges the fundamental assumption in the AI industry that agent benchmarks conducted in isolation accurately predict real-world performance.
Microsoft’s own testing yielded similar disappointing results. Researchers built a synthetic marketplace called the “Magentic Marketplace” to test AI agent behavior, with 100 customer-side agents interacting with 300 business-side agents. The experiments using models like GPT-4o, GPT-5, and Gemini-2.5-Flash found agents were vulnerable to manipulation and overwhelmed by having too many options . The agents also struggled with collaboration without explicit instructions.
A separate benchmark called the Remote Labor Index (RLI) showed that current AI agents perform poorly when automating real remote jobs, with top models automating only 2.5% or less of complex work valued at over $140,000.
Harvard Business Review reached a complementary conclusion: agents aren’t ready for consumer-facing work but can excel at internal processes . The analysis suggests agents work better for internal workflows where errors can be caught and corrected, rather than customer-facing interactions where mistakes directly impact brand and revenue.
Even the mainstream press is noticing. The Hill reported that “AI agents aren’t replacing remote workers any time soon,” citing the mounting evidence of performance limitations.
This reality check sets the stage for everything else that happened in November. The industry is building infrastructure for agents that don’t yet exist as promised capabilities—but the gap between vision and reality is becoming clearer.
Microsoft’s Agent Operating System While studies showed agents struggling in practice, Microsoft made its biggest bet yet on the agentic future. At its Ignite 2025 conference, the company unveiled a comprehensive vision to turn Windows into an “agentic OS” with Agent 365 as the management layer.
Agent 365 is a control plane framework for businesses to securely deploy, manage, and monitor AI agents “like they do people.” The platform provides dashboards, telemetry, and security controls for managing fleets of AI bots. A Microsoft executive quoted in CNBC predicted a future where companies use far more AI agents than human employees.
The portfolio Microsoft announced is extensive:
Agent 365: The central management platform for AI agents across the enterprise Fara-7B: A 7-billion parameter AI agent designed to perform complex computer tasks directly on a user’s device; rivals GPT-4o in benchmark performance and processes data locally for privacy Entra Agent ID: Identity documentation for AI agents, treating them like a digital workforce with their own identities Windows integration: Microsoft is transforming Windows 11 into an “agentic OS” by integrating AI agents directly into the taskbar and File Explorer Magentic Marketplace: An open source simulation environment for testing AI agent behavior Microsoft Foundry: A modular, interoperable, and secure agent stack for building and scaling AI agents eWeek called it “the Operating System for AI Agents.” The vision is clear: Microsoft wants to be the platform layer for the agentic era, just as Windows was for the PC era.
But not everyone is convinced this is what enterprises want. PCMag asked whether anyone actually wants to create their own AI agents, questioning whether the vision aligns with enterprise needs. Computerworld noted the tool is designed to help IT manage “AI agent sprawl”—suggesting agents are proliferating faster than organizations can manage them.
Product Purpose Status Agent 365 Manage AI agents like digital workforce Launched Fara-7B On-device computer-use agent for PCs Launched Entra Agent ID Identity & access control for agents Preview Magentic Marketplace Agent marketplace and testing environment Open Source Copilot Agents Azure agent building tools Updated Microsoft’s announcement also included security tools, reflecting growing awareness of the risks that come with autonomous agents. The company announced autonomous security capabilities for AI agents and partnerships with security vendors like Wiz to secure the agentic environment.
The Ignite announcements weren’t limited to agents—Microsoft also unveiled updates to Azure Copilot agents, AI infrastructure innovations, and integrations with partners like Adobe, Nvidia, ServiceNow, and Workday. But agents were clearly the centerpiece, reflecting Microsoft’s belief that agentic AI represents the next major shift in enterprise computing.
Security Challenges Mount As Microsoft and others build out agent infrastructure, security researchers are documenting serious risks. November brought multiple revelations about how agents can be exploited—or how they can exploit each other.
Documented Attacks The most concerning report came from Axios: Chinese hackers used Anthropic’s Claude Code agent to automate spying operations . The attackers, associated with a group called “Suspended Packages,” used Anthropic’s own AI agent to identify vulnerable files, exfiltrate data, and maintain persistence on compromised systems. This is one of the first documented cases of malicious actors using AI agents as attack tools.
Another concerning finding came from security researchers who discovered that ServiceNow AI agents can be tricked into acting against each other via “second-order prompts.” By crafting prompts that cause one agent to interpret another agent’s actions as hostile, attackers can trigger agent-vs-agent conflicts that disrupt operations.
Medium raised questions about whether Windows 11’s new AI agents represent “convenience or a new attack vector,” noting that agents with deep system access could be exploited if compromised.
Enterprise Readiness Gap Despite these documented risks, enterprises are not prepared. ZDNET reported that “enterprises are not prepared for a world of malicious AI agents,” citing a lack of governance frameworks and security controls. A separate analysis in The AI Economy found that while enterprises anticipate a 2027 AI agent explosion, “reality shows they’re not ready.”
The IAPP (International Association of Privacy Professionals) published two analyses on the topic: one on understanding new risks and practical safeguards and another on considerations for tackling agentic AI risks . Both emphasized that current privacy and security frameworks were not designed for autonomous agents that can access, move, and alter data without human oversight.
CIO summarized the sentiment bluntly: “Agentic AI has big trust issues.”
Security Infrastructure The market is responding with new security tools and frameworks:
Runlayer launched out of stealth with $11 million in seed funding from Khosla Ventures’ Keith Rabois and Felicis. The startup addresses security vulnerabilities in the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the standard for AI agent connectivity. It has already signed eight unicorns as customers .
Ping Identity launched “Identity for AI” , a solution designed to provide identity verification for AI agents in what the company calls the “agent economy.”
Keycard, an AI agent identity startup, acquired Runebook to strengthen its MCP connectivity capabilities.
Nokod Security launched Adaptive Agent Security to protect AI agents across the entire agent development lifecycle.
Wiz unveiled multiple agent security products , including a SecOps AI Agent and AI-SPM for securing AI agents.
AWS published The Agentic AI Security Scoping Matrix , a framework for securing autonomous AI systems.
GitHub published its agentic security principles for building secure AI agents.
Forrester released Applying Forrester’s AEGIS Framework To IAM And AI Agents , a framework for identity and access management in the age of agents.
AvePoint debuted AgentPulse Command Center for AI agent governance.
BleepingComputer explored how “Never Trust, Always Verify” applies to autonomous AI agents.
SlashData published guidance on how to harness AI agents without breaking security .
New America examined privacy and power in the Model Context Protocol era.
Dark Reading warned that “AI Agents Are Going Rogue” and offered strategies to rein them in.
SC Media argued that AI agents could end security’s cycle of toil—if properly managed.
The Hacker News explored how to govern AI agents “from enterprise risk to strategic asset.”
The security challenge is becoming clear: as agents gain more autonomy and access, they become both more valuable and more dangerous. The industry is racing to build guardrails before deployments scale beyond control.
Real-World Deployments Despite the performance limitations and security concerns, real deployments are showing results. The most cited example this month was Klarna, which reported that its AI agent is doing the work of 853 employees . This represents significant productivity—but notably, it’s in customer service, a well-defined domain with clear processes and human oversight available.
Capgemini found that banks and insurers are deploying AI agents to fight fraud and process applications, with plans for new roles specifically to supervise the AI. The report indicates that financial institutions are actively moving key customer-facing processes to AI agents, marking a rapid transformation in how customers interact with banks and insurers. CIO Dive reported that banks are creating “AI supervisor” roles as agent use surges.
Amazon Connect launched AI agents capable of autonomous action for customer service, representing a step beyond simple chatbots toward agents that can take actions on behalf of customers.
In the public sector, Staffordshire Police announced it will trial AI agents on 101 service —the non-emergency police contact line—marking one of the first tests of agents in a government service context. Axios reported exclusively that the IRS has deployed AI agents for internal operations.
Tearsheet podcasted about “AI agents making real financial decisions,” featuring NVIDIA’s Kevin Levitt on the infrastructure behind live deployments at Capital One, Visa, and RBC.
Sage debuted a Finance Intelligence AI Agent for financial workflows. Zeni rolled out an AI agent to automate complex accounting workloads.
Oracle’s Clinical AI Agent clicked quickly for Hudson Physicians, showing results in healthcare. Fast Company explored how AI agents are about to change how people shop, with implications for retail.
The Wall Street Journal reported that “companies begin to see a return on AI agents,” citing early adopters showing measurable ROI. PYMNTS.com published guidance on “What CFOs Should Be Asking About AI Agents,” reflecting finance leaders’ need to understand and justify the investments.
But there are challenges in deployment as well. Ad Age reported on how AI agents are “messing with ad metrics” as Amazon fights Perplexity over undeclared bots. The agents don’t shop like humans, and they don’t view ads like humans—creating measurement headaches for digital advertising.
Company Use Case Results Klarna Customer service Handling work of 853 employees Banks & Insurers Fraud detection & application processing Live deployment with new supervisor roles Staffordshire Police 101 service triage Trial phase IRS Internal operations Deployed Amazon Connect Customer service agents Autonomous action capability The pattern is clear: the deployments that work are specialized, well-defined, and include human oversight. These aren’t autonomous agents replacing humans—they’re tools augmenting humans in specific contexts.
Industry Activity Beyond the headlines, activity continued across sectors:
Financial Services & Commerce Gartner predicted that AI agents will command $15 trillion in B2B purchases by 2028 , representing a massive shift in how business buying happens.
Quantum Metric partnered with Google Cloud to accelerate its push into the AI agent marketplace , leveraging Google’s Gemini and Agent2Agent protocol.
Ad Age reported on how AI agents are threatening retail media ad strategies as Amazon fights Perplexity over undeclared bots.
AWS published on “decoding the future of retail: embracing AI shopping agents.”
The World Economic Forum covered “the rise and risks of AI shopping agents.”
Marketing Brew reported on how brands are aiming to build “algorithmic trust” ahead of an AI agent-powered Black Friday.
PYMNTS.com published on how “AI agents take over the SEO playbook.”
RCR Wireless argued that telecom’s next billion-dollar customer is an AI agent.
Technology Platforms GoDaddy advanced trusted AI agent identity with its Agent Name Service (ANS) API and standards site launch.
Refinder AI Agent brought end-to-end task automation to Slack and Google Chat.
Celonis feeds AI agents with process intelligence data to enhance their operational context.
Everbridge introduced an AI agent in xMatters to accelerate digital service resilience.
Komodor extended its autonomous AI agent for optimizing Kubernetes clusters.
Gluware tackled AI agent coordination with its Titan platform.
WorkFusion partnered with Allied Engineering Group to expand AI agent adoption across the Middle East and Africa .
Fujitsu discussed pioneering the future of business with generative AI and AI agents.
Technology Development NVIDIA published on building an interactive AI agent and how to build and run secure, data-driven AI agents .
MIT researchers developed an AI agent that learns to use CAD to create 3D objects from sketches.
EPAM mapped the GenAI coding landscape, identifying five types of AI agents in the development stack.
DevOps.com covered AI agent performance testing in the DevOps pipeline.
Salesforce unveiled a simulation environment for training AI agents called DreamGym.
AWS introduced Strands Agent SOPs —natural language workflows for AI agents.
SAP Signavio launched Agent Mining to transform enterprise AI.
Deutsche Telekom announced AI agents for mobile networks.
CX Today published on how AI co-pilots are powering the next generation of “super agents.”
Sector-Specific Infosys developed an AI agent to enhance operations in the energy sector.
Supply & Demand Chain Executive covered readying AI agents for procurement.
Crowe examined AI agents as the next shift in manufacturing.
Bloomberg reported that China’s top companies are focusing on AI agents as the next battleground.
CIO provided a change management guide for preparing workforces for AI agents.
S&P Global found that AI agents worsen IT’s capacity crunch.
Infrastructure & Tooling New Agent Launches Neuron7 launched Neuro , a next-gen AI agent for mission-critical service resolution.
Ironclad unveiled its next wave of AI agents for legal agreements.
Cresta unveiled four products at Cresta Wave for human and AI agent collaboration.
Smartsheet unveiled its AI agent platform to elevate productivity and collaboration.
Writer announced AI agents that can “actually do your work—not just chat about it.”
Time Magazine launched an AI-driven interactive agent, with Axios reporting exclusively on the launch.
Intuit introduced a virtual team of AI agents to help UK businesses increase efficiency and growth.
ECI Software Solutions launched a built-in ecommerce AI agent.
Ingram Micro launched an AI agent in its Xvantage platform.
Platform & Tool Updates Google Cloud updated its AI Agent Builder with new observability dashboard and faster build-and-deploy tools.
InfoWorld reported on Google boosting Vertex AI Agent Builder.
Google announced the Agent Development Kit for Go.
Google DeepMind released SIMA 2 , a Gemini-powered AI agent for 3D virtual worlds.
Google published on building AI agents with Gemini 3 and open source frameworks.
Google rolled out new guardrails for AI agents.
Databricks added customizable evaluation tools to boost AI agent accuracy.
AWS showcased enterprise AI agent solutions with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
AWS explained how Letta builds production-ready AI agents with Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL.
Oracle announced its AI Agent Marketplace.
InfoWorld published on the anatomy of an AI agent knowledge base.
The Journal of Accountancy covered creating an AI agent in ChatGPT.
Anthropic published on code execution with MCP for building more efficient AI agents.
The New Stack examined why load tests lie about AI agent performance.
Market Infrastructure IAB launched a technical standard for faster, AI agent-friendly ad auctions. Measuring What Works As enterprises deploy agents, they’re discovering that measurement and governance are prerequisites for success.
Snowflake proposed a “GPA framework” for evaluating AI agent reliability, treating agent assessment like academic grading with metrics across multiple dimensions of performance.
SaaStr reported on 125 days and 750,000 uses of AI agents, concluding that while agents are now “truly part of the team,” their moats are “real but weak.” The same analysis noted that SaaStr runs 20+ AI agents and found their competitive advantages are modest.
MarTech reported that “most AI agents fail without data and governance maturity,” emphasizing that technical capability alone doesn’t ensure successful deployment.
McKinsey published “The state of AI in 2025: Agents, innovation, and transformation,” providing a comprehensive overview of enterprise AI adoption. A separate McKinsey report, “Agents for growth” , examined turning AI promise into business impact.
AP News published a reality check titled “‘Agentic’ AI is a buzzword made up of marketing fluff and real promise,” distinguishing between hype and actual capability.
CIO explored measuring and scaling AI agent value beyond productivity gains.
IBM published on “Enterprise AI Agents: Beyond Productivity,” arguing that value comes from rethinking workflows, not just automating existing tasks.
ERP Today covered how AI agents are shifting from hype to enterprise workflow redesign.
DataRobot argued that IT needs to manage AI agents like a workforce.
The Takeaway November 2025 was a reality check month for AI agents. The hype is meeting reality in three important ways.
First, agents work in narrow contexts with human oversight, not as autonomous replacements. The Upwork study, Microsoft’s marketplace test, and the Remote Labor Index all show the same thing: current AI agents struggle independently but excel with human partners. The deployments that work—Klarna’s customer service agent, banks using AI for fraud detection, Amazon Connect’s autonomous agents—are specialized tools, not general-purpose replacements.
Second, Microsoft’s infrastructure bet suggests the company sees this as a long-term play requiring new OS-level capabilities. Agent 365, Fara-7B, Entra Agent ID, and the Windows “agentic OS” transformation represent a massive investment in the agent platform layer. This is infrastructure build-out, not breakthrough capability. Microsoft is building the roads before the cars are ready.
Third, security challenges are real and escalating. Documented cases of Chinese hackers using Anthropic’s agent for automated spying and ServiceNow agents being tricked into fighting each other show that autonomous agents create new attack surfaces. The rapid emergence of security startups like Runlayer, Nokod, and established players like Wiz and Ping Identity launching agent security products indicates this will be a significant growth area.
The deployments that show results share common characteristics: well-defined domains, clear processes, abundant training data, and human oversight. These aren’t the science fiction autonomous agents that make decisions without context—they’re specialized tools that excel at specific tasks.
Gartner’s $15 trillion prediction for B2B purchases by AI agents in 2028 shows the stakes. But enterprises anticipating a 2027 agent explosion may be premature. The AI Economy found that organizations aren’t ready for the risks.
We’re in the infrastructure build-out phase, not the autonomous agent phase. Forrester’s 2026 predictions underscore that this is a multi-year transition. The winners will be companies that focus on practical deployment in narrow contexts, build robust governance frameworks, and integrate agents as collaborators rather than replacements.
The age of AI agents is coming. But November 2025 showed it’s coming more slowly—and more collaboratively—than the hype suggested.
title: AI Agents in November: The Reality Check

As NeurIPS 2025 approaches, researchers from SAKURA internet and Kyoto University will present MatPROV—a dataset that extracts material synthesis procedures from literature as structured directed graphs using large language models.
This comprehensive review covers 1 article published in November 2025, examining how natural language processing can unlock procedural knowledge trapped in scientific literature.
The Research: Structuring Synthesis Knowledge A paper from SAKURA internet Research Center has been accepted for the AI4Mat Workshop at NeurIPS 2025, introducing MatPROV—a dataset that applies large language models to the challenge of extracting material synthesis procedures from scientific literature.
The research team, led by Hirofumi Tsuruta and Masaya Kumagai from SAKURA internet (with Kumagai also affiliated with Kyoto University), will present their work on December 6, 2025, at the AI4Mat Workshop in New Orleans.
What MatPROV Does MatPROV addresses a fundamental problem in materials science: synthesis procedures exist as unstructured text in scientific papers—paragraphs describing multi-step workflows in inconsistent formats across thousands of publications. This makes it difficult for AI systems to learn from historical data or plan new syntheses.
The MatPROV approach uses large language models (LLMs) to parse natural language descriptions of material synthesis and convert them into structured representations. Specifically, the output is a directed graph where nodes represent materials and operations, and edges capture dependencies between steps.
The PROV-DM Standard What distinguishes MatPROV from other extraction efforts is its use of the PROV-DM (Provenance Data Model) standard. PROV-DM is a W3C recommendation for representing provenance information—the lineage of entities, activities, and agents involved in producing a piece of data.
In the context of materials synthesis, PROV-DM provides a formal way to represent:
Entities: The materials, reagents, and equipment involved Activities: The processing steps, reactions, and transformations Agents: The researchers, instruments, or automated systems performing actions Derivations: How output materials derive from input materials This standardized representation enables computational analysis, similarity search between procedures, and integration with laboratory automation systems.
Component Description Input Unstructured synthesis procedures from scientific literature Extraction Method Large language models (LLMs) parse natural language text Data Standard PROV-DM (W3C Provenance Data Model) Output Format Structured directed graphs (nodes: materials/operations, edges: dependencies) Application Electronic laboratory notebooks, AI-driven synthesis planning Research Team and Affiliations The paper comes from SAKURA internet Inc., a Japanese internet infrastructure company that has established a research center working at the intersection of cloud computing and materials informatics. The dual affiliation of Masaya Kumagai—SAKURA internet and Kyoto University—reflects the collaboration between industry and academia that characterizes much of the materials informatics field.
Why This Matters: The Synthesis Bottleneck Materials discovery has advanced rapidly on the computational side—property prediction from composition and structure is now routine for many material classes. But synthesis planning remains largely manual, dependent on expert knowledge buried in literature.
The Unstructured Knowledge Problem Consider a typical synthesis paper: a paragraph might describe heating precursors to a specific temperature, holding for a duration, cooling at a controlled rate, then performing a characterization step. The procedure spans multiple sentences, uses domain-specific terminology, and embeds critical parameters within narrative text.
For an AI system to learn from this, it needs to:
Identify that this is a synthesis procedure (not background or results) Extract each discrete operation Understand which materials are inputs and outputs for each step Capture parameter values (temperatures, times, concentrations) Represent the sequence and dependencies correctly MatPROV tackles this by leveraging LLMs’ natural language understanding capabilities, combined with the formal structure of PROV-DM, to create a standardized representation.
From Text to Graph: The MatPROV Pipeline Scientific Paper Text | v LLM Parsing (identify procedures, extract entities) | v PROV-DM Mapping (assign roles: entity, activity, agent) | v Directed Graph (nodes and edges) This graph representation enables several applications:
Computational analysis: Compare procedures across papers, identify common patterns Similarity search: Find synthesis methods that use similar approaches Integration with ELNs: Electronic laboratory notebooks can automatically capture provenance Automation potential: Structured graphs can be converted to executable scripts for robotic labs NeurIPS and AI4Mat: A Prestigious Venue The acceptance of this work to the AI4Mat Workshop at NeurIPS 2025 signals that the research meets technical standards for contribution in the machine learning community.
NeurIPS (Neural Information Processing Systems), established in 1987, is the premier machine learning conference. Acceptance to the main conference or its workshops requires peer review and technical rigor. The AI4Mat Workshop, started in 2022, specifically focuses on applying machine learning to materials science problems.
This venue matters because it brings materials informatics to the mainstream ML community. The workshop audience includes both materials scientists seeking ML tools and ML researchers looking for applications—exactly the interdisciplinary audience for provenance-aware materials data.
The workshop format allows for focused discussion on challenges specific to materials ML: small datasets, complex physics, and the need for interpretable models that scientists can trust.
Looking Ahead: From Papers to Pipelines What are the potential impacts if the MatPROV approach scales across the materials literature?
Potential Applications Large-scale synthesis analysis: With thousands of procedures extracted as structured graphs, researchers could analyze patterns across material classes, identifying which synthesis routes are most common or which parameters correlate with successful outcomes.
Robotic laboratory integration: Structured procedure graphs can be converted to executable automation scripts. A robot could read a synthesis graph, map operations to available equipment, and execute the procedure automatically.
Improved electronic laboratory notebooks: ELNs that automatically capture provenance would make experiments more reproducible. Instead of free-form notes, the notebook would maintain a formal graph of what was done, with what, by whom, and when.
ML models on structured data: Models trained on structured procedure representations could learn to predict synthesis conditions for new materials, rather than just predicting properties from composition.
Challenges to Address The research faces several challenges:
Extraction accuracy: LLMs can miss domain-specific nuances or misinterpret procedural language Terminology diversity: Different communities use different terms for similar operations Scaling to diverse materials: Ceramics, polymers, and metals each have specialized synthesis techniques Validation: How to verify that extracted graphs accurately represent the intended procedure A Quiet Month, A Steady Advance November was notably quiet for major materials discovery announcements. This single accepted paper highlights an important truth: fundamental research infrastructure—datasets, standards, extraction methods—often advances steadily between headline-grabbing discoveries. The work that enables the next generation of AI-driven materials labs happens incrementally, paper by paper, workshop by workshop.
MatPROV is one step toward making materials synthesis knowledge computable. Whether this particular approach scales remains to be seen, but the direction—using LLMs to extract structured, standards-compliant representations from literature—will likely influence how materials informatics bridges the gap between published knowledge and automated discovery.
title: NeurIPS 2025: MatPROV Dataset Structures Materials Synthesis Knowledge for AI
