Company Amount Focus Coralogix $115M Observability AI agent Commure $200M Healthcare workflow agents Sema4.ai $25M AI agent platform Sedai $20M Cloud optimization agents Veris AI $8.5M Simulated training for agents Industry Applications Healthcare Healthcare emerged as a key vertical for AI agent deployment, with applications ranging from administration to patient outreach.
Empara launched a voice AI agent to boost healthcare service efficiency for administrators. Infinitus deepened its partnership with Salesforce to accelerate AI agent adoption in healthcare and life sciences.
Saifr launched a new AI agent for insurance companies. Workday outlined AI agent trends and use cases in healthcare.
Finance & HR Financial services firms are adopting AI agents after seeing benefits from AI chatbots. PYMNTS.com reported on banks adopting AI agents following chatbot success. Intuit rolled out AI agents for QuickBooks to tackle CRM, finance, and CX tasks, as covered by CMSWire .
Mercer analyzed how AI agents can revolutionize pension markets, while Workday focused on agents transforming HR operations.
Legal The legal sector is seeing competition between Microsoft and Google for small law dominance. LawSites analyzed the battle for small law dominance in the AI agent era. Thomson Reuters explored how agentic AI is redefining the legal profession.
Retail & Real Estate Collov AI launched the world’s first listing marketing AI agent for real estate. INSEAD Knowledge analyzed how AI agents are rewriting retail power.
Other retail coverage included MarketingProfs on what marketers need to know and Digiday on creators using agentic AI for fan engagement.
Government & Public Sector Route Fifty provided a transformation guide for state and local agencies. FedScoop reported the CIA considers AI agents “the most exciting AI trend.” Federal News Network covered how AI agents could rescue federal acquisition.
Additional Vertical Coverage Marketing: ADWEEK on PMG using AI agents for Fox News ad targeting; Salesforce on reducing rote marketing tasks; AdExchanger on marketing to machines Supply Chain: Supply Chain Digital on Zip’s 50 AI agents for procurement; Supply Chain Digital on CH Robinson’s shipping classification agent Telecommunications: Vodafone Idea and telco AI agents Food & Restaurant: Restaurant Business on how AI agents might change what we eat Defense: FlightGlobal on Saab’s AI agent trial for Gripen E fighter Cross-Industry Insights McKinsey examined the future of customer experience with agentic AI. MarTech explored what AI agents really do for customer experience. ERP Today covered NTT DATA’s strategic Agentforce play.
Developer & Coding Agents New Tools The developer tools ecosystem expanded rapidly in June with new coding agent offerings.
Google’s Gemini CLI launch was covered by ZDNET as bringing Gemini to the command line. Microsoft released a free 1-hour course to build your first AI agent.
Cursor launched a web app to manage AI coding agents. Pythagora introduced specialized AI agent teams to transform “vibe coding” . GitHub unveiled a prototype for autonomous bug fixing.
Warp introduced an agentic development environment to help developers work with AI coding agents. The creator of Spring Java unveiled an AI agent framework for the JVM. GitHub also published documentation on assigning and completing issues with its coding agent.
Effectiveness & Best Practices Developers debated the effectiveness of coding agents in June. Timothy B. Lee documented what he learned trying seven coding agents. Zencoder examined whether pair programming with AI coding agents is beneficial.
Towards Data Science provided a developer’s guide to building scalable AI with workflows versus agents. Another Towards Data Science article showed how to build an AI agent to explore data catalogs with natural language.
Architecture & Orchestration Technical discussions covered how AI agents communicate and coordinate. Towards Data Science explained how AI agents “talk” to each other. IBM covered multi-agent orchestration for productivity.
MIT Media Lab published research on levels of agentic coordination from tools to crowds. Netguru examined when to use multi-agent systems versus solo agents.
Security Concerns WIRED reported that AI agents are getting better at writing code and hacking it as well. Hackernoon outlined 15 principles to deliver AI agents to production.
Additional Developer Coverage NVIDIA showed how to build efficient AI agents through model distillation. The New Stack covered how frontier firms are revolutionizing DevOps with AI agents.
Platforms & Infrastructure The infrastructure layer for AI agents expanded significantly in June, with launches across cloud providers, enterprise software companies, and vertical specialists.
Major Platform Launches Databricks launched Agent Bricks , a no-code AI agent builder. KPMG launched KPMG Workbench , a multi-agent AI platform, with additional coverage from Inside Public Accounting .
Workday expanded its AI agent partner ecosystem with a new program and introduced an agent gateway that adds third-party AI agents to its agentic landscape.
IBM made its API Agent generally available in IBM API Connect. MuleSoft introduced Connect AI for orchestrating secure AI agents at scale.
Amazon open sourced the Strands Agents SDK for building AI agents.
Vertical Platforms Amplitude launched AI agents to speed up product decision-making. Vanta launched an AI agent to automate compliance workflows. BrowserStack launched a suite of AI agents to redefine software quality at scale.
Cresta launched an intelligent omnichannel AI agent . Lumos launched Albus , the world’s first AI agent for autonomous identity governance. LocaliQ launched a voice AI agent to transform prospect conversations.
Infobip debuted an AI agent platform . Pegasystems expanded features to build and manage AI agents.
Additional Infrastructure HPE Aruba touted new AI agents and a network orchestrator. HPE also launched GreenLake Intelligence , adding AI agents throughout its hybrid cloud stack.
Okta debuted Cross App Access to secure AI agent interactions. Genesys introduced an AI Studio for a “grown-up path” to agentic AI.
Snowflake added agentic products and AI-ready data to its marketplace. Adobe expanded its suite of AI agents with Product Support and Data Insights agents.
Oracle & AWS Oracle continued expanding its agentic offerings with an Analytics Cloud Gen AI Agent and OCI Generative AI Agents integration with Oracle APEX. Oracle also covered using Intelligent Advisor with Fusion AI Agent Studio.
AWS published guidance on building intelligent AI voice agents with Pipecat and Amazon Bedrock; empowering AI agents with user context using Amazon Cognito; using AI agents with Amazon SES ; and building multi-agent business experts using Amazon Bedrock.
Other Platform Announcements kama.ai made Cohere available on its Hybrid AI Agent Platform Uzabase announced Speeda AI Agent , a specialized AI agent for business insights Totvs launched an AI agent strategy to bolster cloud subscriptions IBM expanded OpenPages 9.1.1 with AI agent capabilities Synapxe unveiled platforms to scale system-wide innovation Company Platform Key Feature Salesforce Agentforce 3 Observability, MCP support Databricks Agent Bricks No-code builder KPMG Workbench Multi-agent platform Workday Agent Gateway Third-party agent integration Google Gemini CLI Terminal-based AI agent IBM API Agent API Connect integration Amazon Strands SDK Open source agent framework Research & Experiments Experimental Deployments Anthropic’s “Project Vend” documented whether Claude could run a small shop. The research report and Futurism coverage described unintentionally hilarious results as the AI agent struggled with basic retail operations. Anthropic also published how it built its multi-agent research system.
Nature published research on the development and validation of an autonomous AI agent for clinical decision-making in oncology, representing significant progress in medical AI applications.
WIRED explored practical agent applications with articles on unpacking AI agents and letting AI agents plan vacations .
Academic Research MIT Technology Review questioned whether we’re ready to hand AI agents the keys. MIT also examined how AI agents can learn to reason like humans.
Anthropic published research on agentic misalignment , exploring how LLMs could become insider threats.
Explainer Articles Several outlets published comprehensive explainers about AI agents. CNET explained what agentic AI is. Wavestone published an agentic AI playbook. RealEstateNews.com covered what to know about AI agents.
Use Cases and Examples FutureScot provided a guide to leveraging AI agents for public services. Mashable listed seven popular AI agents widely used by companies. CIO outlined nine promising use cases for business.
NVIDIA showed how to scale realistic robot simulation using the NeMo Agent Toolkit for physical AI. AutoGPT listed 20 AI agent examples in 2025.
Industry Analysis KDnuggets questioned if it’s too early or already behind for AI agents in analytics workflows. Salesforce Agentforce 3 coverage focused on visibility. Bernard Marr argued AI agents are the missing link between enterprise ambition and execution.
Interoperability & Standards Efforts to standardize agent communication accelerated in June, aimed at preventing ecosystem fragmentation.
Google and the Linux Foundation pushed the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol to enable agent-to-agent communication. Towards Data Science explained the protocol’s design. TechRepublic reported that the vendor-neutral interoperability project’s participants include Microsoft, Google, AWS, and Salesforce. SDxCentral covered the open standard push.
Security concerns accompanied the interoperability push. TrendMicro warned that a classic MCP server vulnerability can undermine entire AI agent ecosystems.
IBM covered how AI agents collaborate and the world of multi-agent orchestration. Amazon Bedrock showed how to build an intelligent multi-agent business expert.
China’s AI Agent Boom China’s AI agent ecosystem developed in parallel to Western efforts, with local companies launching distinct offerings.
MIT Technology Review reported that Manus has kick-started an AI agent boom in China. China Daily covered Laiye launching an enterprise-level AI agent matrix.
ZTE accelerated AI agent innovation with its AI Agent Factory Co-Sight solution. Caixin Global published an in-depth analysis describing AI agents as triggering the next tech battlefield in China.
Rest of World reported that China is gaining ground in the global race to develop AI agents. Yum China rolled out an AI agent to help rather than replace store managers.
Looking Ahead June’s developments paint a complex picture of agentic AI’s trajectory. Platforms are launching rapidly, enterprises are investing heavily, and use cases are proliferating across industries. Yet the research reveals significant reliability gaps that must be addressed.
The Tension Between Hype and Reality ZDNET argued AI agents will be ambient but not autonomous. VentureBeat suggested agent-based computing is outgrowing the web as we know it. Yet Bernard Marr highlighted five AI agent myths that need to be debunked.
Oracle positioned agentic AI as the next big thing in artificial intelligence, while CIO clarified how AI agents and agentic AI differ from each other.
Workforce Transformation The workforce implications of AI agents received significant attention. TechRadar considered whether we’re ready to welcome AI agents as team members. Workday explored how AI agents are reshaping work, roles, and strategy. IT Brief Australia emphasized balancing innovation with responsibility.
McKinsey explored seizing the agentic AI advantage. Another McKinsey piece declared the future of work is agentic.
Strategic Guidance For business leaders, CIO provided guidance on scaling AI agents for business. TechTarget examined AI agents as increasingly viable for enterprise use.
Substack covered the AI agent architecture debate. The AI Journal argued AI agents are the future of business process automation.
The Path Forward The World Economic Forum suggested agentic AI will revolutionize business in the cognitive era. IBM examined when AI agents join the org chart.
The research from Carnegie Mellon, Stanford, Salesforce, and Gartner suggests that while agentic AI holds tremendous promise, current limitations are significant. The ~70% error rate on multi-step tasks, the 65% failure rate on multiturn CRM tasks, and Gartner’s prediction that 40% of projects will be scrapped by 2027 all point to the need for realistic expectations.
Yet the enterprise momentum is undeniable. RSM’s $1 billion commitment, the major platform launches from Salesforce, Google, and Microsoft, and the expanding use cases across industries all signal that organizations see enough value to continue investing despite the limitations.
Success in this environment will likely require: human oversight for high-risk workflows; clear use cases that match agent capabilities; realistic expectations about reliability; investment in observability and monitoring; and gradual scaling from low-risk to higher-risk applications.
The gap between platform marketing and proven capability remains significant. But as the research benchmarks improve and enterprises learn where agents can deliver real value versus where they cannot, the industry should move toward more mature implementations. The companies that succeed will be those that balance enthusiasm for the technology’s potential with clear-eyed assessment of its current limitations.
title: AI Agents in June 2025: Platforms Launch as Studies Question Reliability

content:
IBM announced a roadmap to build the world’s first fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029, declaring that “the science is solved.” Meanwhile, researchers demonstrated breakthroughs in error correction that could reduce overhead by 20x, and IonQ went on a $1.4 billion acquisition spree. The quantum computing industry isn’t just promising the future anymore—it’s building it.
This comprehensive review covers 145 articles published between June 1-30, 2025, surveying a landscape of roadmaps, breakthroughs, and strategic consolidations that suggest quantum computing is entering an engineering phase.
The Big Story: IBM’s 2029 Roadmap to Fault Tolerance IBM declared on June 10 that the fundamental science behind fault-tolerant quantum computing is solved , unveiling a concrete roadmap to build a practical quantum supercomputer by 2029. The announcement marks a shift in how the industry talks about quantum computing—from scientific challenge to engineering problem.
The centerpiece of IBM’s roadmap is Starling, a system that will use approximately 10,000 physical qubits to create 200 logical qubits—error-corrected qubits that can perform reliable computations. IBM says Starling will be capable of 100 million quantum operations and will be 20,000 times more powerful than current quantum computers.
The breakthrough enabling this roadmap is a new approach to error correction called quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. These codes allow for 9x more efficient hardware scaling than traditional surface codes, dramatically reducing the number of physical qubits needed for each logical qubit.
Beyond Starling: Blue Jay and the Path Forward IBM’s roadmap extends beyond 2029. The company plans Blue Jay, a system with 2,000 logical qubits capable of 1 billion quantum operations, targeted for 2033. This kind of scaling would enable quantum computers to tackle problems in chemistry, materials science, and optimization that are intractable for classical supercomputers.
The roadmap includes intermediate milestones:
2025: The Flamingo processor with 156 logical qubits 2026: The Kookaburra modular processor with error-corrected capabilities 2029: Starling with 200 logical qubits (~10,000 physical qubits) 2033: Blue Jay with 2,000 logical qubits IBM’s Jay Gambetta, vice president of quantum operations, stated that the company has moved from “proving the science” to “scaling the technology.” The roadmap is built on IBM’s Heron architecture (156 qubits released in 2024) and the new Loon QPU architecture featuring qLDPC-based couplers.
Skepticism and Validation Not everyone is convinced. Some researchers point out that IBM hasn’t yet demonstrated a 200-logical-qubit system, and the jump from today’s 50-logical-qubit record (held by Quantinuum) to 200 is substantial. The company’s track record includes missing previous timelines, though IBM has consistently delivered new processors on its roadmap.
However, the technical details in IBM’s peer-reviewed preprint uploaded to arXiv on June 2-3 provide substance to the claims. The qLDPC codes enable a physical-to-logical qubit ratio of roughly 50:1, compared to 1,000:1 or worse for surface codes.
Error Correction Breakthroughs While IBM was announcing its roadmap, researchers around the world were demonstrating breakthroughs in error correction—the technical challenge that makes fault tolerance possible. Three advances in June suggest the resource overhead problem is solvable.
Magic State Distillation Revolution Osaka University researchers developed a new approach to preparing “magic states”—special quantum states required for fault-tolerant quantum computing. Their “level-zero” method reduces the spatial and temporal overhead of magic state distillation by roughly 20x (some coverage says “several dozen times”).
Magic states are essential for implementing the full set of quantum gates required for universal quantum computing. Traditional magic state distillation is expensive, consuming thousands of physical qubits and many rounds of computation. The new approach requires far fewer qubits and rounds, addressing what the researchers call “the core challenge of noise.”
The team, led by Tomohiro Itogawa and Keisuke Fujii, published their work in PRX Quantum. Their simulations show that the level-zero technique could dramatically accelerate the timeline for practical quantum computers by reducing one of the largest resource overheads in fault-tolerant architectures.
Separately, researchers at Quantinuum demonstrated magic state generation on the company’s ion-trap quantum computers, producing high-quality states using just 8 qubits in one study—far fewer than previously thought necessary.
Microsoft’s 4D Geometric Codes Microsoft revealed a family of four-dimensional geometric codes that can reduce error rates by up to 1,000x while requiring 5-6x fewer physical qubits per logical qubit than surface codes.
The codes use a “twisted torus” architecture that enables single-shot error checking—detecting and correcting errors in one operation rather than multiple rounds. This approach is particularly well-suited for qubit modalities with all-to-all connectivity, such as neutral atoms and ion traps.
Microsoft demonstrated the codes in collaboration with Atom Computing, using their neutral-atom qubits to create and entangle 28 logical qubits with error detection and correction capabilities. The partnership aims to scale to 50 logical qubits in the near term.
The specific implementation uses a [[96,6,8]] code—96 physical qubits encoding 6 logical qubits with a code distance of 8. This achieves a logical error rate of \(10^{-6}\) with a physical error rate of \(10^{-3}\), representing a significant improvement over surface codes.
Hardware-Integrated Error Correction Nord Quantique, a Canadian startup, demonstrated a “bosonic qubit” with error correction built directly into the hardware. The approach uses multimode encoding in a superconducting aluminum cavity to achieve a 1:1 physical-to-logical qubit ratio—dramatically more efficient than the 50:1 or 1,000:1 ratios required by other approaches.
The company claims a future 1,000-logical-qubit machine could break an 830-bit RSA encryption key in one hour using only 120 kilowatt-hours of energy. By comparison, a supercomputer would require nine days and 280,000 kilowatt-hours.
Nord Quantique plans to release a 100-logical-qubit machine by 2029 and a 1,000-logical-qubit machine by 2031, with a footprint of just 215 square feet. The company demonstrated 32 rounds of error correction without measurable decay in qubit state.
Approach Organization Key Innovation Improvement Level-zero magic states Osaka University Simplified preparation method 20x overhead reduction 4D geometric codes Microsoft Twisted torus architecture 1,000x error reduction Bosonic qubits Nord Quantique Logical qubit in single hardware 2,000x lower power Scaling the Hardware: Cryogenics and Control Building large-scale quantum computers requires solving the “wiring problem”—how to control thousands of qubits at milli-kelvin temperatures without generating excess heat. Two breakthroughs in June addressed this challenge.
Cryogenic Control Chips Researchers at the University of Sydney, in collaboration with Diraq and Emergence Quantum, demonstrated a CMOS-based control chip that operates at cryogenic temperatures within less than 1mm of qubits with negligible fidelity loss.
The team reported no reduction in coherence time for single- and two-qubit operations, validating the integration of complex electronics with fragile spin qubits at near absolute zero. The cryogenic control system operates within a 10-microwatt power envelope—critical for not disrupting the milli-kelvin environment required for quantum computation.
This breakthrough, published in Nature, provides a pathway for building quantum processors with millions of qubits by enabling control electronics to be placed directly on the quantum chip rather than connected via room-temperature electronics through bulky coaxial cables.
The work represents more than a decade of research led by Professor David Reilly, with the chip designed by Dr. Kushal Das and experiments led by Dr. Sam Bartee. The collaboration included industry partners Emergence Quantum and Diraq, aiming to use existing CMOS manufacturing technology for scalable quantum processors.
Efficient Readout Amplifiers Chalmers University of Technology researchers developed a pulse-operated quantum amplifier that activates only during qubit readout, reducing power consumption to just one-tenth of the best current amplifiers.
The amplifier responds to incoming qubit pulses within 35 nanoseconds, cutting average power consumption by 86-90%. By activating only when needed, the amplifier reduces heat-induced decoherence and enables more qubits per system.
The team, led by doctoral student Yin Zeng and professor Jan Grahn, used genetic programming to optimize the amplifier’s performance. The work was conducted in collaboration with Low Noise Factory AB and supported by the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology.
This advance addresses a critical bottleneck: readout amplifiers operating continuously at cryogenic temperatures generate heat that limits how many qubits can be integrated into a single system. By reducing power consumption by 90%, the amplifier enables significantly larger quantum computers.
Demonstrating Quantum Advantage June brought multiple demonstrations of quantum computers outperforming classical systems—not on contrived benchmark problems, but on tasks with practical relevance.
Theoretical Breakthrough: Unconditional Quantum Speedup Researchers from the University of Southern California and Johns Hopkins University demonstrated the first unconditional exponential quantum speedup , using two 127-qubit IBM Quantum Eagle processors to solve a variation of Simon’s problem.
What makes this result significant is the word “unconditional.” Previous quantum advantage demonstrations, including Google’s 2019 quantum supremacy claim, relied on specific sampling problems where classical verification was difficult. This demonstration on a well-understood theoretical problem provides a clean proof that quantum computers can exponentially outperform classical ones for certain tasks.
The team used advanced error mitigation techniques, including dynamical decoupling and measurement error mitigation, to achieve the result on current noisy hardware. Daniel Lidar, Viterbi Professor of Engineering at USC and cofounder of Quantum Elements Inc., emphasized that while this is a key proof-of-principle, it doesn’t yet solve a practical real-world problem.
Simon’s problem is a foundational problem in quantum algorithms related to the Abelian Hidden Subgroup Problem. The exponential speedup demonstrates that quantum computers can solve certain problems with exponentially fewer operations than any known classical algorithm.
Practical Applications University of Vienna researchers demonstrated that photonic quantum computers can enhance machine learning algorithms , using just two photons to outperform classical algorithms for kernel-based machine learning tasks. The team, led by Philip Walther, showed potential energy efficiency benefits alongside computational advantages.
The research, published in Nature Photonics, used a novel photon injection process with six distinct configurations. The approach could enhance performance in fields like natural language processing and help identify tasks where quantum computers excel in hybrid systems.
IonQ, in collaboration with AstraZeneca, AWS, and NVIDIA, announced a quantum-accelerated drug discovery workflow that achieved a more than 20x speedup in time-to-solution for simulating a Suzuki-Miyaura reaction. The hybrid quantum-classical workflow integrates IonQ’s Forte QPU with NVIDIA GPUs via AWS services, reducing a key drug development step from months to days.
NVIDIA partnered with Ansys and DCAI to advance quantum algorithms for fluid dynamics on the CUDA-Q platform using the Gefion supercomputer. The collaboration enables GPU-accelerated simulations of Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Methods, allowing researchers to study quantum applications in computational fluid dynamics.
Teleportation and Networking Oxford University physicists achieved teleportation between quantum computers for the first time , using quantum teleportation to create a working logic gate between two separate chips six feet apart.
The demonstration, led by physicist Dougal Main, achieved 86% fidelity in recreating spin states via teleportation. The team successfully ran Grover’s search algorithm on the distributed gate with a 71% success rate, pointing to a strategy of distributing quantum workloads across multiple small processors linked by teleportation.
This approach could overcome stability issues that limit single quantum computers and enable scalable, robust quantum computing systems. The work builds on earlier demonstrations of qubit teleportation over fiber networks (27 miles in a 2020 experiment) but is the first to implement a logic gate via teleportation between separate quantum processors.
Industry Consolidation: IonQ’s Buying Spree IonQ spent over $1.4 billion in June 2025 on two acquisitions that signal a maturing quantum computing market and a shift toward full-stack quantum platforms.
The Oxford Ionics Acquisition On June 9, IonQ announced it would acquire UK-based Oxford Ionics for $1.075 billion—$1.065 billion in IonQ common stock and $10 million in cash.
Oxford Ionics, founded by Dr. Chris Ballance and Dr. Tom Harty, brings “ion-trap-on-a-chip” technology that combines trapped-ion performance with semiconductor manufacturing scalability. The acquisition adds 80 experts to IonQ’s team.
The combined company released ambitious projections:
2026: Systems with 256 physical qubits at 99.99% accuracy 2027: Systems with over 10,000 physical qubits at 99.99999% logical accuracy 2030: Systems with 2 million physical qubits and 80,000 logical qubits at 99.9999999999% accuracy The transaction reinforces IonQ’s commitment to its Bothell, Washington manufacturing facility, where the company plans a $1 billion investment in the Pacific Northwest over the next decade.
The Lightsynq Acquisition Earlier in the month, on June 3, IonQ completed the acquisition of Lightsynq Technologies , a startup specializing in photonic interconnects and quantum memory. The deal brought key talent and over 20 patents to IonQ’s portfolio.
Founded by Dr. Mihir Bhaskar, Dr. Bart Machielse, and Dr. David Levonian, Lightsynq’s technology accelerates IonQ’s roadmap toward modular quantum architectures and the development of a quantum internet. The acquisition adds capabilities in:
Photonic interconnects for linking quantum processors Quantum memory for storing quantum information Quantum repeater technology for long-distance quantum networking Together, the acquisitions position IonQ as a full-stack trapped-ion quantum computing company, combining hardware expertise with networking capabilities. This follows similar consolidation trends in classical computing, where companies vertically integrated to control the entire technology stack.
Additional Capital Raises Rigetti Computing raised $350 million through an at-the-market (ATM) stock offering, bringing its total cash reserves to approximately $575 million with no outstanding debt. The funds will expand Rigetti’s superconducting quantum hardware and invest in manufacturing.
The capital raises suggest quantum computing companies are positioning for commercial markets, not just research. Investors are supporting scale-up efforts as the industry transitions from scientific prototypes to engineered systems.
Acquirer Target Value Technology IonQ Oxford Ionics $1.08B Trapped-ion systems IonQ Lightsynq Undisclosed Photonic interconnects, quantum memory Global Competition: China’s Photonic Push China launched its first production line for next-generation photonic chips , using thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) to create 6-inch wafers with performance exceeding global benchmarks.
The pilot line, built by Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s CHIPX, achieves 110 GHz modulation bandwidth—breaking a key technical barrier. The facility has an annual capacity of 12,000 wafers, enabling rapid iteration and potential commercial supply.
The production line aims to achieve technological self-reliance and accelerate development in AI, quantum computing, and 6G networks. The facility uses 110 advanced fabrication tools and represents 15 years of research led by professor Jin Xianmin.
China also unveiled the ez-Q Engine 2.0, a quantum control system designed to support quantum computers with over 1,000 qubits—marking it as the world’s third-largest quantum platform behind IBM and Atom Computing. The system, delivered to key research institutions, features:
Support for 5,000 qubits in control services 504-qubit superconducting quantum computer for testing Domestic components reducing reliance on foreign technology Origin Quantum, a Chinese startup, used its superconducting quantum processor to enhance breast cancer screening accuracy, demonstrating practical medical applications. The country is rapidly building a quantum computing industrial ecosystem, with the market projected to grow over 30% annually, reaching 11.56 billion yuan by 2025.
The geopolitical dimension is clear: China is pursuing a different technological approach (photonics vs. superconducting/trapped-ion) while investing heavily in domestic capabilities. This parallels similar competition in AI semiconductors and classical computing.
Research Roundup: Other Notable Advances Protein Folding and Drug Discovery Researchers used a 36-qubit trapped-ion quantum computer from IonQ to solve protein folding problems for peptides up to 12 amino acids—the largest such demonstration on trapped-ion hardware to date. The team used a novel algorithm called BF-DCQO and also successfully applied it to MAX 4-SAT and spin-glass problems.
A study in Nature Scientific Reports described a quantum-enhanced intelligent system for personalized adaptive radiotherapy dose estimation, integrating quantum algorithms with deep learning to achieve 8-15x computational speedups and 50-70% reduction in mean absolute error.
Power Grid Optimization IonQ and Oak Ridge National Laboratory researchers developed a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm to solve the power grid “unit commitment” problem, demonstrating solutions within 0.55% to 2.7% of optimal cost for grids with up to 26 generators. The approach combines a quantum variational algorithm to search generator states with classical optimization.
Trapped-Ion Advances Researchers at the Quantum Systems Accelerator advanced trapped-ion quantum computing with a new chip holding up to 200 ions, demonstrated parallel gate operations and multi-qubit entanglement techniques, and implemented mid-circuit measurements for verifiable quantum advantage. The “enchilada trap chip” operates with RF voltages from 150V to 300V.
PsiQuantum researchers published a study outlining a path to loss-tolerant photonic quantum computing using fusion-based quantum computing (FBQC), with some designs achieving up to 18.8% loss tolerance.
UK Government Investment The UK government committed £670 million to quantum computing research and development, reinforcing the country’s position as a leader in trapped-ion technology and supporting companies like Oxford Ionics (prior to its acquisition by IonQ).
Healthcare Applications A study on quantum computing in healthcare noted that most applications remain theoretical, with practical implementation facing challenges in qubit quality, error correction, and algorithm development. However, the field is showing promise in drug discovery, medical imaging, and treatment optimization.
Cosmic Ray Errors Research confirmed that cosmic rays cause errors in superconducting qubits, presenting a challenge for large-scale quantum computing that will require shielding or error-correction strategies to overcome.
Looking Ahead: From Promise to Platform June 2025 may be remembered as the month quantum computing transitioned from scientific curiosity to engineering discipline. The roadmap announcements, error correction advances, and industry consolidation suggest a field maturing from research prototypes toward engineered systems.
The timeline for fault-tolerant quantum computing shifted from “someday” to “2029”—IBM’s explicit deadline. The breakthroughs in magic states (20x overhead reduction), 4D geometric codes (1,000x error reduction), and hardware-integrated error correction (1:1 physical-to-logical ratio) suggest the resource overhead problem is solvable through multiple technical approaches.
The acquisitions suggest companies are positioning for commercial markets, not just research. IonQ’s $1.4 billion spending spree builds a full-stack trapped-ion platform with networking capabilities. Rigetti’s $350 million capital raise funds superconducting hardware development.
But challenges remain. IBM hasn’t demonstrated 200 logical qubits yet, and skepticism about timelines persists. The gap between roadmap projections and current capabilities is substantial—from 50 logical qubits today to 200 by 2029, and from 1,000 physical qubits to 10,000.
The geopolitical competition with China’s photonic investments adds urgency. Different technological approaches (superconducting, trapped-ion, photonic) are racing toward fault tolerance, with national security implications and economic stakes measured in the hundreds of billions of dollars.
What’s clear is that quantum computing is no longer just about qubit counts or quantum supremacy benchmarks. It’s about building reliable systems that can solve practical problems in chemistry, materials science, optimization, and machine learning. The focus has shifted from proving quantum computers work to making them useful.
Company June Development Why It Matters IBM Starling roadmap announced Clearest timeline to fault tolerance IonQ Two major acquisitions Building full trapped-ion stack Microsoft 4D error codes revealed Alternative path to fault tolerance Nord Quantique Bosonic qubit demo Hardware-integrated error correction Rigetti $350M capital raise Funding superconducting roadmap The question for the rest of 2025 and beyond: Can the industry execute on these ambitious roadmaps? The science may be solved, as IBM claims, but the engineering work has only just begun.
title: June 2025: The Month Quantum Computing Grew Up

content:
This comprehensive review covers 17 articles published during May 2025, surveying how AI is transforming materials science from a trial-and-error discipline into a predictive science. Researchers demonstrated autonomous XRD analysis at synchrotron speeds, established a scaling law for simulation-to-real transfer learning, and screened 121 million molecules for battery applications using GPU acceleration. Perhaps most significant is the validation of a new scaling law showing how computational databases can overcome experimental scarcity - providing a quantitative roadmap for the field.
Methods: AI Tools That Scale The most significant methodological advance this month came from CrystalShift, a new probabilistic algorithm for autonomous X-ray diffraction phase labeling and lattice refinement. Published in npj Computational Materials on May 24, the method combines symmetry-constrained optimization, best-first tree search, and Bayesian model comparison to estimate probabilities for phase combinations - all without requiring training data. This addresses a key bottleneck in high-throughput experimentation: determining crystal structures from XRD data at synchrotron speeds. By enabling AI-powered autonomous materials discovery, CrystalShift provides the rapid, automated analysis needed for closed-loop experimentation systems.
Also on May 24, Nature published work establishing a power-law scaling relationship for simulation-to-real (Sim2Real) transfer learning in materials science. The study demonstrated that prediction error on real systems decreases as computational data increases - following a predictable scaling law. Researchers validated this behavior across 70,000 amorphous polymers from the RadonPy dataset and 130,000 small organic molecules from the QM9 database. The practical significance is clear: the scaling behavior helps determine necessary sample sizes and equivalent experimental data, guiding computational database development for real-world applications. This tells us quantitatively how much computational data we need to trust predictions about physical materials.
Cornell University researchers added efficiency to this scaling equation. In work published May 19 , the team demonstrated knowledge distillation techniques that create faster, smaller AI models for molecular property prediction, alongside a physics-informed generative AI framework for designing realistic crystalline materials. Perhaps most forward-looking is their exploration of “generalist materials intelligence” - systems that function as autonomous research assistants rather than single-purpose tools. Together, these three advances show a maturing field: we’re building tools that are both autonomous and efficient.
Discoveries: New Materials from AI Search AI search engines are finding genuinely new material classes, not just optimizing known ones. At the Chinese Academy of Sciences, researchers used an interpretable machine learning framework to discover a new family of infrared functional materials called selenoborate halides with the chemical formula ABa₃(BSe₃)₂X. Published May 9, the work overcomes traditional trial-and-error methods by identifying materials that exhibit a balanced set of properties including wide bandgaps and strong second harmonic generation - demonstrating a complete pathway for AI-driven design of functional crystal materials.
Magnetic Materials Renmin University of China developed an AI-based search engine called MatAltMag that identified 50 new altermagnetic materials - including the first four i-wave types ever discovered. The research, published in National Science Review on May 16, uses pre-training and fine-tuning with graph neural networks to predict magnetic properties from symmetry analysis. Perhaps most striking is the scope of the problem: only 2% of magnetic materials have experimentally confirmed magnetic structures, leaving vast territory for AI exploration. The same platform also predicted the high-temperature superconductor Li₂AuH₆ with a transition temperature of 140 K under ambient pressure.
Quantum Materials Rutgers University researchers discovered intercrystals - a fundamentally new class of materials where electronic properties are controlled by moiré patterns from twisted graphene layers. Published May 21, the discovery enables geometric control over electron behavior that could advance quantum computing, atomic sensors, and low-loss electronics. Led by Board of Governors Professor Eva Andrei, the work extends twistronics beyond two-dimensional materials into a broader materials design paradigm.
Structural Materials Virginia Tech and Johns Hopkins University researchers developed a new multiple principal element alloy with enhanced strength using explainable AI and data-driven frameworks. The approach uses evolutionary algorithms and SHAP analysis to provide interpretable insights into material properties. Published May 15 and funded by the NSF, the work demonstrates how AI can transform traditional trial-and-error methods in metallurgy into a predictive science.
Energy Applications: Catalysts, Batteries, Thermal Management Hydrogen Production A research team at Tohoku University’s Advanced Institute for Materials Research developed a closed-loop framework called DigCat for accelerating catalyst discovery. The platform identified RbSbWO₆ as a promising bifunctional catalyst for acidic water splitting - remaining stable in acidic conditions where many catalysts degrade. Published May 29, the approach combines digital tools with experiments to efficiently find materials for clean hydrogen production, potentially reducing reliance on expensive noble metals.
Battery Materials Three advances this month addressed different aspects of battery technology. The University of Texas at Dallas researchers discovered that mixing two solid electrolytes creates a “space charge layer” at their interface that unexpectedly enhances ion movement. Published May 30, the finding provides a new design strategy for improving solid-state batteries, which promise to be safer and store more than twice the power of conventional lithium-ion batteries. The work is part of the BEACONS initiative, a $30 million effort funded by the Department of Defense.
SES AI and NVIDIA announced a partnership on May 8 to map the “Molecular Universe” of potential battery electrolyte materials. Using NVIDIA’s ALCHEMI, cuML, H100/A100 GPUs, and NeMo Framework, they screened 121 million molecules and achieved an 80x acceleration of machine learning and DFT calculations. The partnership estimates 100 billion to 1 trillion possible electrolyte materials exist - a search space that would require thousands of years without AI acceleration.
Researchers from the University of Chicago, University of California San Diego, and Ningbo Institute of Materials Technology & Engineering discovered a material that can restore used EV batteries to like-new performance through voltage activation. Published May 20, the breakthrough uses negative thermal expansion and oxygen-redox electrochemistry to create metastable states - potentially revolutionizing the second-hand electric car market where 75% of UK drivers express serious concerns about battery degradation.
Heat Management CU Boulder researchers observed destructive phonon interference at room temperature for the first time - a phenomenon where thermal vibrations interfere like sound waves to cancel heat flow. Published May 6 in Nature Materials, the team developed an ultra-sensitive thermal probe to demonstrate this “muting” effect at the molecular scale. This discovery unlocks precise control of heat dissipation in future electronics, enabling thermal management at the molecular level.
Sustainability: Low-Carbon Materials Researchers published a data-driven screening method in Nature Communications Materials on May 17 that identifies alternative cementitious materials to reduce concrete’s carbon footprint. Cement production accounts for more than 6% of global greenhouse gas emissions, and traditional clinker substitutes have decreased in availability by 37% over two decades. The team used large language models to extract data from 88,000 academic papers, identifying 14,000 materials and training a neural network on 318 samples to predict reactivity. Their analysis found that waste materials and natural rocks could replace 50% of global cement production - cutting associated emissions by 3%, equivalent to removing 260 million vehicles from U.S. roads.
Fundamental Physics: Light into Solids For the first time, scientists at Italy’s National Research Council successfully transformed light into a supersolid - a state of matter exhibiting both the rigid structure of a solid and the frictionless flow of a superfluid. Published May 12, the achievement uses precisely controlled laser light and polaritons to validate theoretical predictions dating back to the 1970s. This provides a real-world platform for studying exotic quantum states, with potential applications in quantum computing and ultra-precise sensing technologies.
Business: Funding and Partnerships These technical advances are attracting significant commercial investment and partnership activity.
Materials Nexus, a London-based startup, is preparing to raise up to $30 million in Series A funding to expand its materials discovery service into the U.S. market, with a particular focus on data centers. The round is expected to launch later in 2025.
The SES AI-NVIDIA partnership demonstrates commercial scaling of GPU-accelerated materials discovery. Beyond the technical achievement of screening 121 million molecules, the collaboration signals how cloud computing infrastructure is becoming integral to materials research.
Texas A&M assistant professor Dr. Daniel Tabor received the 2025 JPC C Lectureship Award from the American Chemical Society for his work using AI to predict and design new materials for batteries, solar cells, and electronics. His perspective, published May 20, addresses whether AI means the end of test tubes and beakers - concluding that computational methods accelerate discovery but experimental validation remains essential.
Nanyang Technological University professor Eliodoro Chiavazzo presented on AI tools for energy materials on May 28, introducing the Energy GNoME platform for bias-corrected generative AI. His work focuses on metal-organic frameworks for thermal energy storage - addressing a challenge where 40% of global energy consumption and 36% of CO₂ emissions come from heating and cooling buildings.
Platform Developer Application Scale CrystalShift Researchers Autonomous XRD analysis Synchrotron speeds MatAltMag Renmin University Altermagnetic materials 50 new materials found DigCat Tohoku University Catalyst discovery Closed-loop framework Molecular Universe SES AI/NVIDIA Battery electrolytes 121M molecules screened Energy GNoME NTU Energy materials Bias-corrected generative AI Looking Ahead The Sim2Real scaling law published this month provides a theoretical foundation for why these AI methods work - and tells us quantitatively how much computational data we need to trust predictions about physical systems. This transforms computational databases from reference libraries into training data for predictive models.
We’re seeing a transition from individual AI tools to integrated platforms: DigCat for catalysts, MatAltMag for magnetic materials, Molecular Universe for electrolytes, Energy GNoME for energy materials. The business activity suggests commercial scaling is underway, with startups raising capital and big tech partnerships bringing GPU infrastructure to materials discovery.
The question facing the field is how the role of human scientists evolves. Cornell’s “generalist materials intelligence” concept hints at AI as research assistant rather than replacement - handling the routine tasks of data analysis and screening while humans provide the scientific judgment about what problems are worth solving and what discoveries matter. The most successful systems this month combined both: autonomous AI doing the heavy lifting of screening and prediction, guided by human scientific understanding of what to look for and why it matters.
title: AI Acceleration: May 2025 in Materials Discovery

May 2025 brought significant advances in quantum error correction, with multiple research groups demonstrating techniques that could dramatically reduce the resources needed for fault-tolerant quantum computing. At the same time, new systems came online, major funding rounds were announced, and the industry continued to mature with strategic partnerships and acquisitions. This comprehensive review covers 198 articles published in May 2025.
Error Correction Advances Qudit Correction Breaks New Ground Researchers at Yale University have demonstrated the first experimental quantum error correction for qudits —quantum systems with more than two levels. The team achieved error correction for both qutrits (3-level systems) and ququarts (4-level systems) using the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) bosonic code, surpassing the break-even point for the first time in higher-dimensional quantum information processing. The experiment, published in Nature , achieved performance gains of 1.82 ± 0.03 for qutrits and 1.87 ± 0.03 for ququarts.
This approach leverages the larger Hilbert space of higher-dimensional quantum systems, potentially enabling more hardware-efficient error correction. The researchers used a reinforcement learning agent to optimize the system and employed the small-big-small (SBS) protocol with echoed conditional displacement (ECD) gates. Key specifications included a cavity energy relaxation lifetime of 631 microseconds and cavity Ramsey coherence time of 1,030 microseconds.
Bosonic Codes Show Promise Nord Quantique announced results from its multimode encoding approach using a bosonic Tesseract code, demonstrating no measurable decay over 32 correction cycles . The technique uses a 1:1 ratio between physical cavities and logical qubits, dramatically reducing the physical qubit overhead typically required for error correction.
The company projects that systems with over 1,000 logical qubits could occupy just 20 square meters by 2029. For the RSA-830 benchmark, the approach demonstrated a 99.6% reduction in power consumption compared to classical HPC—120 kWh projected versus 280,000 kWh for conventional methods. The system achieved a 1 MHz clock speed, providing an efficiency edge over many competing approaches.
RSA Attack Requirements Drop Craig Gidney, a researcher at Google Quantum AI, has published a revised estimate for the resources needed to crack RSA-2048 encryption. The new analysis indicates that fewer than 1 million physical qubits could break a 2048-bit RSA key in less than a week—a 95% reduction from the 20 million qubit estimate Gidney published in 2019.
The improvement stems from advances in approximate modular exponentiation, layered error correction, and optimized quantum operations. The study assumes a surface code cycle time of 1 microsecond, maximum gate error rate of 0.1%, and approximately 6.5 billion Toffoli gate operations requiring about 5 days of continuous operation. This puts increased pressure on organizations to accelerate migration to post-quantum cryptography, with NIST recommending deprecation of vulnerable systems after 2030 .
Additional Error Correction Advances Infleqtion, in collaboration with JPMorgan Chase, has released an open-source quantum error correction library called qLDPC that implements low-density parity check codes. The library can reduce the number of physical qubits needed per logical qubit by a factor of 10 to 100—from approximately 1,500 physical qubits per logical qubit to just 15-150 physical qubits.
Researchers also published work on concatenated codes combining C4/C6 codes with quantum Hamming codes , which reduces space overhead by over 90% compared to surface codes for logical error rates of 10^-10 and 10^-24, while achieving a high threshold of 2.5%. This protocol is particularly suited for quantum architectures with all-to-all connectivity, such as neutral atoms and trapped ions.
New Systems and Milestones Commercial Systems Launch D-Wave announced general availability of the Advantage2 quantum computer , featuring 4,400+ qubits and operating at 12.5 kilowatts of power consumption. The sixth-generation system has processed 20.6 million customer problems on prototypes since June 2022, with usage increasing 134% in the past six months. The system is available through D-Wave’s Leap cloud service in 40 countries with 99.9% availability, and can also be deployed on-premises at customer facilities.
Equal1 launched the Bell-1 quantum server , the world’s first silicon-based quantum computer that is rack-mountable and plugs into a standard power outlet. The six-qubit system weighs 440 pounds (200 kg) and operates at 0.3 kelvin, using a self-contained cooling unit that eliminates the need for specialized infrastructure. The design integrates classical processors with quantum processor units on a single chip, allowing deployment in existing data centers.
Quandela launched the Belenos photonic quantum computer , featuring a doubling of qubit count and a 4,000× power increase compared to its predecessor.
In China, Origin Quantum released the Tianji 4.0 , a superconducting quantum measurement and control system that supports over 500 qubits. The Origin Wukong quantum computer, powered by Tianji technology, has served users in 139 countries and regions, completing 380,000 quantum computing tasks across industries like finance and biomedicine since beginning operation in January 2024.
National Deployments IQM Quantum Computers signed an agreement with Finland’s VTT Technical Research Centre to deliver a 150-qubit system in mid-2026 and a 300-qubit system in late 2027 . The 300-qubit system will be the largest superconducting quantum computer procured to date and is purpose-built for quantum error correction research. The project builds on previous deliveries of 5-qubit, 20-qubit, and 50-qubit systems to VTT.
QuEra Computing installed its first quantum computer outside its own labs at Japan’s National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST). The gate-based neutral-atom system will be integrated with the NVIDIA-powered ABCI-Q supercomputer as part of Japan’s national quantum strategy. Japanese Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba declared 2025 “the first year of quantum industrialisation.”
In Italy, the first IQM quantum computer was activated in Turin at Politecnico di Torino. The five-qubit system operates at 20 millikelvin, occupies 4 square meters, and stands 3 meters tall. IQM has also signed an agreement with CINECA to integrate a 54-qubit Radiance quantum computer with the Leonardo supercomputer by Q4 2025.
India is deploying its largest quantum computer, an IBM Quantum System Two with a 156-qubit Heron processor , in Amaravati through collaboration between IBM, TCS, and the Andhra Pradesh government. The Quantum Valley Tech Park is scheduled to open in January 2026.
Performance Benchmarks Quantinuum announced that its H2 system has achieved a Quantum Volume of 8,388,608 (2^23) , the highest reported QV to date. This milestone concludes the company’s five-year commitment to increase QV tenfold annually. The company’s next-generation Helios system is expected to surpass H2 in scale and fidelity.
Company/Org System Qubits Key Features Timeline D-Wave Advantage2 4,400+ Annealing, cloud/on-prem GA May 2025 Equal1 Bell-1 6 Silicon, rack-mountable Launched IQM Finland system #1 150 Superconducting Mid-2026 IQM Finland system #2 300 Superconducting Late-2027 Origin Quantum Tianji 4 500+ Measurement & control May 2025 Quandela Belenos TBD Photonic, 4,000x power May 2025 Funding, Acquisitions, and Partnerships Strategic Acquisitions IonQ announced its intention to acquire Lightsynq , a startup specializing in photonic interconnects and quantum repeaters. Lightsynq brings a team of experts from Harvard and AWS, along with a portfolio of over 20 quantum memory patents. The acquisition positions IonQ to pursue modular scaling toward millions of qubits and to develop quantum internet infrastructure. IonQ’s current Forte systems feature 36 algorithmic qubits, with roadmap targets scaling to the 10,000s and ultimately to millions of qubits.
Major Funding Rounds NVIDIA is in advanced talks to invest in photonic quantum computing startup PsiQuantum , marking the GPU giant’s first direct bet on hardware qubits. The potential investment would value PsiQuantum near $6 billion in a $750 million funding round led by BlackRock. PsiQuantum aims to build a million-qubit fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2028 using photonic integrated circuits fabricated in commercial CMOS lines. The company has previously secured $940 million from Australia and over $500 million from the State of Illinois for its quantum campus.
Classiq Technologies raised $110 million in a funding round led by Entrée Capital, bringing total capital raised to $173 million. The Israeli quantum software startup aims to become the “Microsoft of quantum computing” by providing a universal software platform for quantum applications. The funding will support global expansion and workforce growth from 65 to 130 employees. This represents part of a broader surge in Israeli quantum funding, with $289 million raised by Israeli quantum computing startups in 2025 compared to $82 million in 2024.
Maryland Governor Wes Moore has committed $1 billion over five years to establish the state as the “‘Capital of Quantum’” through a combination of state funding and federal matching. The initiative includes up to $100 million in matching contributions each from DARPA and Maryland through 2029, plus $10 million in state funding for IonQ’s new headquarters in College Park and an additional $5 million in economic development funds.
Other significant funding announcements include Alice & Bob building a $50 million quantum lab in Paris and Quobly raising €21 million for development of a 100-qubit silicon chip.
Strategic Partnerships Invest Qatar entered a strategic partnership with Quantinuum to strengthen the country’s quantum ecosystem. The agreement includes tailored support services, joint research initiatives, and educational programs. This follows the launch of Qatar’s first quantum computing laboratory at Hamad Bin Khalifa University under the QC2 initiative, supported by a $10 million research grant from Qatar’s Ministry of Defence.
Kvantify, a Danish quantum software company, will use the AI supercomputer Gefion to simulate quantum computers at scale for quantum chemistry and drug discovery. This marks the first time a dedicated quantum software company leverages Gefion’s exaflop-class performance. The collaboration enables large-scale simulations of industry-relevant molecules like penicillin using hundreds of qubits.
Honda and Quemix co-developed a quantum state readout technology that “scans” classical data features from a quantum state without causing collapse. The partners performed the world’s first practical XAFS computation for materials development on an actual quantum computer using logical qubits, aiming to accelerate research into energy materials for carbon neutrality by Honda’s 2050 target.
In India, the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) inaugurated the Quantum Technology Research Centre in Delhi , focused on developing sovereign quantum technologies for defense applications including secure communications, sensing, and precision timing.
Miami University and Cleveland Clinic are partnering to establish Ohio’s first specialized quantum computing degree programs and research experiences, leveraging Cleveland Clinic’s IBM Quantum System One—the world’s first quantum computer dedicated to healthcare research.
Research Frontiers Error Sources and Mitigation A study published in Nature has directly observed that cosmic-ray muons and gamma-rays cause quasiparticle bursts in superconducting qubits, leading to large-scale correlated errors that are devastating for quantum error correction. Researchers separated the contributions of muons (18.4%) and gamma-rays (81.6%) and demonstrated that monitoring charge-parity jumps provides a highly sensitive method for detecting these bursts. The study, which used a 63-qubit superconducting processor with 31 qubits selected for measurement, estimates that muon-induced bit flips occur approximately every 25 minutes.
This research highlights a fundamental obstacle to practical fault-tolerant quantum computing with superconducting qubits. DARPA is currently investigating which quantum approaches can overcome these correlated error challenges.
Qubit Platform Advances Silicon spin qubits continue to gain ground as a leading candidate for scalable quantum computing. A review in Intelligent Computing details advances in gate-defined and donor-based quantum dots, highlighting 0.5 second coherence times and 99.95% single-qubit gate fidelity. The technology’s compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing enables potential operation above 1 Kelvin (“hot qubits”), which would significantly reduce cooling requirements.
Researchers at the University of Oxford have developed a novel experimental technique, the Andreev STM, to definitively identify intrinsic topological superconductors . The technique confirmed uranium ditelluride (UTe2) as an intrinsic topological superconductor, accelerating the search for materials that can host stable, topologically protected qubits. This could enable the discovery of simple, inexpensive crystalline materials to replace complex synthetic structures.
Researchers from the University of Illinois Chicago demonstrated that combining Majorana edge modes and Majorana zero modes in two-dimensional topological superconductors provides a platform for efficient fault-tolerant quantum gates. The work shows how Majorana edge modes can function as memory elements, simulating key quantum operations through many-body dynamics.
MIT researchers developed a new superconducting circuit component called the “quarton coupler” that enables record-breaking interaction between light and matter, potentially making quantum operations and readout up to 10 times faster—allowing for more error correction within qubits’ limited coherence time.
Researchers at Florida State University discovered exotic states of matter in graphene , including integer and fractional quantum anomalous Hall states that allow electrons to flow without resistance at zero magnetic field. The discovery was made by engineering five-layer graphene structures with boron nitride at ultra-low temperatures.
Algorithms and Applications A benchmarking study published in Nature demonstrated that quantum annealing with advanced hardware and hybrid techniques outperforms classical solvers for large-scale combinatorial optimization problems. The quantum solver achieved approximately 0.013% higher accuracy and was about 6,561 times faster than the best classical solver on a 10,000-variable problem, solving it in 0.0854 seconds.
Researchers used quantum computing and generative machine learning to design novel KRAS inhibitors for cancer treatment . The hybrid AI framework screened over 1 million molecules, identifying 15 candidates, two of which showed binding and functional activity in cellular assays. The work used Quantum Circuit Born Machines (QCBMs) combined with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks.
Australian researchers used a trapped-ion quantum computer and a novel mixed qudit-boson simulation technique to model how real molecules change after absorbing light. The approach is at least 1 million times more resource-efficient than standard quantum methods, successfully simulating light-induced dynamics in three molecules using far fewer qubits and entangling operations.
Researchers introduced AdaBoost.Q, a quantum adaptation of the AdaBoost algorithm , achieving over 86% accuracy on a ten-class MNIST task and 100% accuracy on a quantum feature recognition task using a programmable superconducting processor.
IBM released a quantum optimization benchmarking library (QOBLIB) with 10 problem instances to advance the field. Researchers also developed a greedy gradient-free adaptive VQE algorithm that demonstrates noise resistance for near-term quantum devices.
Other research advances include:
Quantum computing predicting particle trajectories in optical tweezers using linear combination of unitaries Synthesis of a reversible quantum Vedic multiplier on IBM quantum computers with significant reductions in quantum cost First end-to-end QEC pipeline for molecular energy on Quantinuum H2-2 Lockheed Martin and IBM combining quantum with classical HPC using SQD Networking and Communication Researchers have demonstrated universal distributed blind quantum computing with solid-state qubits , enabling secure quantum computations where the client’s data remains private from the server.
Scientists in the U.K. successfully connected two quantum processors using existing fiber optic cables for the first time. The experiment in distributed quantum computing allowed the processors to share resources and operate as a single entity, transmitting photons, quantum information, and a quantum algorithm (Grover search).
Researchers from the University of Geneva demonstrated that joint quantum measurements can be performed on separate particles without physical proximity, as long as measurement devices share entangled particles. They developed a classification system that maps measurement types to the required entanglement resources.
Materials and Novel Approaches Researchers are exploring the fractional quantum anomalous Hall effect (FQAHE) in materials like twisted bilayer MoTe2 and rhombohedral multilayer graphene as a pathway to create topological qubits with intrinsic fault tolerance. The work outlines two potential routes to achieve Z3 parafermions, which are necessary for universal topological quantum computation.
Researchers have proposed a complete architecture for fault-tolerant continuous-variable quantum computation based on a 2D spatiotemporal cluster state. The architecture combines a biased Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code with a repetition code, achieving fault tolerance with a squeezing threshold of 12.3 dB.
Norwegian researchers discovered that common clay exhibits a 2D structure suitable for quantum technology, specifically the mineral dickite, which could enable more affordable production of quantum components.
Ecosystem Expansion New Research Centers Hamad Bin Khalifa University has launched Qatar’s first quantum computing laboratory under the Qatar Center for Quantum Computing (QC2) initiative. The lab is supported by a $10 million research grant from Qatar’s Ministry of Defence and will focus on applied research in quantum algorithms, error correction, cryptography, and benchmarking.
India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) inaugurated the Quantum Technology Research Centre in Delhi , focused on developing sovereign quantum technologies for defense applications like secure communications, sensing, and precision timing.
Global Quantum Developments The United Nations has declared 2025 the International Year of Quantum Science and Technology, with 14 countries submitting the resolution and 70 countries backing it. In a historic milestone, researchers in South Africa achieved the first quantum satellite communication in the southern hemisphere, setting a record for the longest intercontinental link at 12,900 km. South Africa’s Department of Science and Technology has provided ZAR142 million (USD $7.8 million) in funding for the South African Quantum Technology Initiative over five years.
Africa’s quantum ambitions are expanding, with continental collaboration and national strategies emerging to develop a quantum economy. The African Quantum Consortium (AQC) hosted an online roundtable in March 2025, and the Quantum Science and Technology Across Africa conference is scheduled for June 2025 at the University of KwaZulu-Natal.
Policy and Industry Analysis The U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency’s 2025 Worldwide Threat Assessment warns that quantum technologies , particularly sensors and secure communications, are nearing battlefield relevance as China and Russia make significant advances. The report highlights that quantum sensing could undermine traditional stealth and navigation capabilities.
Science News examined “the second quantum revolution” as quantum mechanics turns 100 years old, tracing its origins to Werner Heisenberg’s 1925 work and highlighting current efforts to precisely control quantum phenomena for building quantum computers, sensors, and communication networks.
Wipro released analysis on quantum computing becoming a scaled solution, while Live Science published a primer on quantum computing facts for general audiences. Silicon Quantum Computing CEO Michelle Simmons discussed the industry landscape on Bloomberg.
Looking Ahead May’s developments underscore a key theme in quantum computing: multiple approaches to error correction are showing improved efficiency simultaneously. From Yale’s qudit demonstration and Nord Quantique’s bosonic codes to Infleqtion’s qLDPC library and Google’s revised RSA attack estimate, the field is finding ways to reduce the overhead required for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
Hardware diversification continues with no clear winner yet. Silicon spin qubits gain ground due to semiconductor compatibility; photonic systems attract major NVIDIA investment; annealing systems from D-Wave reach general availability; neutral atoms from QuEra deploy internationally; and trapped-ion systems from Quantinuum set benchmark records. This experimentation suggests the market may support multiple specialized architectures rather than converging on a single technology.
Strategic consolidation through acquisitions like IonQ-Lightsynq and partnerships like Honda-Quemix shows investor confidence maturing beyond early hype. Government investments are moving from announcement to deployment: Finland’s 300-qubit system is contracted for 2027, India’s IBM system is deploying, and Maryland’s $1 billion initiative is executing.
The timeline to useful quantum computers remains long, but the path is becoming more concrete. Error correction requirements are decreasing; hardware options are expanding; and funding is flowing to both research and commercialization. The question is shifting from “when” to “what applications first” as focus narrows to optimization, chemistry simulations, and materials science as potential early advantage domains.
Challenges remain: cosmic rays cause correlated errors in superconducting arrays; scaling from hundreds to millions of qubits requires modular approaches; and post-quantum cryptography migration timelines are compressing. But May’s progress suggests the field is making tangible advances on the technical obstacles that have long separated quantum promise from practical reality.
title: Quantum Error Correction Breakthroughs, New Hardware Milestones, and Major Funding Announcements Highlight May's Developments
