Google dropped A2A, an open protocol for AI agents to talk to each other. Microsoft says every worker will soon be an “agent boss” managing AI teammates alongside human colleagues. Visa and Mastercard are preparing for AI shopping agents. Meanwhile, CIOs are asking: Is this real or just hype?
This comprehensive review covers 185 articles published in April 2025, surveying the rapidly evolving AI agent landscape. Major tech firms unveiled competing visions for how autonomous AI will transform enterprise work, protocol wars emerged, and security partnerships formed to address enterprise concerns.
The Protocol Wars Begin The most significant technical development of April was Google’s launch of A2A (Agent-to-Agent), an open protocol designed to enable AI agents to communicate directly with each other. Announced on April 9 , A2A addresses a fundamental bottleneck in multi-agent systems: interoperability.
The protocol allows AI agents from different developers and platforms to exchange information and coordinate actions without requiring custom integrations for each pair of systems. This is the foundational infrastructure needed for multi-agent workflows to scale beyond single-vendor ecosystems. As The Stack reported , Google’s announcement immediately sparked a “protocol war” with competing standards.
The competitive landscape includes:
A2A (Agent-to-Agent): Google’s open protocol for universal agent communication MCP (Model Context Protocol): Anthropic’s protocol for connecting AI models to external data sources ACP (Agent Communication Protocol): An alternative approach from other vendors The emergence of multiple competing standards reflects the high stakes. The protocol that achieves broad adoption will shape how agents interact for years to come. Vendors are positioning their protocols as the foundation for enterprise agent ecosystems.
Google complemented the A2A announcement with new agent building tools and an open source framework added to Vertex AI for building agents. These tools give developers practical ways to implement A2A in their applications.
Enterprise interest in agent interoperability is real. TCS partnered with Google Cloud on A2A interoperability to help enterprises build “future-ready” agent systems. The partnership signals that large systems integrators are already preparing to implement agent-to-agent communication for their clients.
The protocol question remains unresolved. Which standard will win? The answer may come down to which vendor can attract the most developer adoption and enterprise partnerships. Google’s first-mover advantage with A2A is significant, but Anthropic’s MCP has gained traction through its integration with popular AI models. The next few months will be critical in determining which protocol becomes the de facto standard for agent communication.
Microsoft’s Agent Boss Future Microsoft made its clearest statement yet on AI agents in April: every human worker will soon be an “agent boss” , managing AI teammates alongside human colleagues. This isn’t framed as incremental productivity improvement—it’s presented as an org chart transformation.
The vision comes from Microsoft’s 2025 Work Trend Index, which highlights how AI agents are reshaping the future of work . Microsoft envisions a workplace where each employee manages a team of AI agents, with human-to-agent ratios becoming a critical metric for organizational success. As Constellation Research reported , these ratios “will be critical to success as new roles emerge.”
The practical implementation involves several new capabilities:
Azure AI Foundry received new capabilities for building advanced agentic applications . The platform now provides unified tooling for developing, deploying, and managing AI agents at enterprise scale. These enhancements aim to simplify the journey from prototype to production for agentic systems.
Agent flows were introduced as a new concept for transforming automation with AI-first workflows . Agent flows provide a visual way to design multi-step workflows where AI agents coordinate with each other and with humans to complete complex tasks.
The Copilot Control System was announced to bring “order and management” to potential AI agent sprawl. As enterprises deploy dozens or hundreds of agents, managing them becomes a challenge—similar to the API sprawl problem of previous decades. The control system provides centralized governance.
Microsoft also announced three new AI agents for autonomous contact centers , targeting customer service as a key use case. These agents can handle routine inquiries, route complex issues to humans, and learn from interactions over time.
Customer deployments show the vision in practice. NTT DATA is transforming its enterprise with agentic AI in Microsoft Fabric and Azure AI Foundry. Roland Berger relies on AI agents and Microsoft Azure to create “more time for value creation.”
Microsoft’s broader messaging frames agentic AI as driving AI-first business transformation . The company’s research division also published on how human-agent teams will reshape the workforce .
Not everyone accepts the “agent boss” framing uncritically. As CIO.com explored , Microsoft sees AI agents shaking up org charts and eliminating traditional functions—but The Guardian noted the uncertainty around what this means for workers. Geekwire characterized the shift as Microsoft seeing “humans as ‘agent bosses,’ upending the workplace.”
Additional Microsoft announcements included new computer use capabilities in Copilot Studio for UI automation, guidance on identifying readiness for AI-first development , and a report on agents of change unlocking potential .
Microsoft also tapped AI agents and partners to scale and automate cybersecurity protections, extending the agentic vision into security operations.
The Great Platform Rush Google wasn’t the only company building agent infrastructure in April. A wave of platform announcements from major vendors revealed a land grab for developer mindshare.
Google’s Double Play Beyond the A2A protocol, Google announced the Agent Development Kit , which lets enterprises “rapidly prototype and deploy AI agents without recoding.” The kit provides pre-built components and templates to accelerate agent development.
Google Cloud also unveiled an AI Agent Marketplace at its Next conference, creating a centralized location for discovering and deploying pre-built agents. The marketplace approach mirrors the app store model, aiming to create an ecosystem around Google’s agent platform.
Nvidia Goes GA Nvidia announced the general availability of NeMo tools for building AI agents . The NeMo Microservices are designed to create an “AI agent data flywheel”—as agents interact with systems, they generate data that can improve future agent performance.
Nvidia also unveiled the AI-Q Blueprint for transforming AI agent systems into digital workforces, and published technical content on building enterprise AI agents with advanced open Llama Nemotron reasoning models.
Enterprise Governance Dataiku introduced AI Agents to unify and govern enterprise agent deployments . The focus on governance reflects enterprise concerns about managing agent sprawl, ensuring compliance, and maintaining oversight as agents proliferate.
**Futurum Group analyzed Oracle’s AI Agent Studio](https://futurumgroup.com/insights/is-oracles-ai-agent-studio-the-missing-layer-for-enterprise-wide-automation/) , positioning it as “the missing layer for enterprise-wide automation.” Oracle’s approach emphasizes unified management and integration with existing enterprise systems.
Other Platform Announcements Writer unveiled “AI HQ” as a platform betting on agents to transform enterprise work Amazon Web Services published on building multi-agent systems with LangGraph and Amazon Bedrock Camunda added AI agents to its process orchestration platform Security: Agents as Threat and Shield AI agents are reshaping cybersecurity in two directions—agents are being deployed to defend against threats, but they’re also creating new attack vectors.
Defensive Agents Security vendors are rapidly incorporating agents into their products:
Vectra AI completed its groundbreaking agent portfolio , positioning its agentic AI systems as “setting new standard” for threat detection and security team efficiency.
Abnormal AI launched breakthrough AI agents to reimagine security awareness training and provide instant board-ready data insights. The agents aim to automate security training while providing executives with visibility into security posture.
Jit launched AI agents to ease AppSec workload , bringing automation to application security testing.
Nvidia published on advancing cybersecurity operations with agentic AI systems and how agentic AI enables the next leap in cybersecurity .
Google, Radiant, and Qevlar expanded AI agent use for SOCs (security operations centers).
Solutions Review catalogued the top AI agents for cybersecurity teams .
Securing the Agents As agents become more powerful, securing them becomes critical:
CyberArk and Accenture partnered to secure enterprise AI agents . The partnership combines CyberArk’s identity security with Accenture’s AI Refinery to address what CyberArk calls identity security for AI agents .
Sentra introduced Data Security for AI Agents as a solution to secure the next generation of business automation .
TechTarget explored how AI agents raise stakes in identity and access management .
CIO Dive reported that IT leaders want better security and data privacy from AI agents.
New Attack Vectors MIT Technology Review warned that cyberattacks by AI agents are coming . The article explores how autonomous AI could be used to conduct more sophisticated, adaptive cyberattacks at scale.
CFO Dive noted that AI agents emerge as potential targets for cyberattackers—a new threat vector where attackers compromise agents themselves to gain access to enterprise systems.
Company Security Focus Approach CyberArk + Accenture Identity Security Partnership Vectra AI Threat Detection AI-Powered Agents Abnormal AI Security Training Awareness Agents Sentra Data Security Agent Protection Jit AppSec Workload Automation Shopping With AI Agents E-commerce is quietly becoming the first major battleground for practical AI agent applications.
Amazon’s new AI agent will shop third-party sites for you . The agent browses external websites to find products, compare prices, and make purchases—extending Amazon’s reach beyond its own marketplace.
Mastercard’s Agent Pay transforms how enterprises use AI search by eliminating window switching. The product enables AI agents to complete purchases directly within enterprise workflows, removing friction between search and transaction.
Visa gives AI shopping agents “intelligent commerce ” capabilities by extending its payment rails to support agent-initiated transactions. AP News reported that Visa “wants to give artificial intelligence ‘agents’ your credit card.”
Visa CMO Frank Cooper III discussed the company’s bet on AI agents in an interview about “culture, commerce and marketing’s next frontier.”
Nvidia explored how AI agents enhance online shopping , outlining use cases for personalized recommendations, automated comparison shopping, and conversational commerce.
These developments point to a future where AI agents become primary participants in e-commerce—representing consumers in transactions, negotiating prices, and making purchasing decisions. The payment networks’ early positioning suggests they see agents as both an opportunity and a threat to existing commerce models.
Healthcare’s Agent Experiment Healthcare emerged in April as a key early adopter of AI agent technology, with several focused deployments in high-value use cases.
Infinitus launched the first trusted voice AI agents for healthcare , targeting administrative workflows like prior authorization and benefits verification.
Cedar rolled out an AI voice agent to tackle patients’ medical billing questions , addressing a major pain point in healthcare finance.
Seattle Children’s teamed up with Google Cloud to develop a decision-support AI agent for healthcare providers. The clinical decision support agent aims to help clinicians access relevant information more quickly.
Google Cloud sees multi-agent AI systems as healthcare’s “next frontier” , expanding AI agent tools for healthcare .
Oracle reported that AI agents show promise in transforming healthcare .
PwC explored how Google Cloud and AI agents transform healthcare .
Relatient launched Dash Voice AI Agent to automate patient appointment management in call centers .
eHealth introduced AI voice agents to enhance customer experience in health plan selection .
Healthcare’s adoption pattern is notable: providers are focusing agents on administrative tasks (billing, appointments, prior authorization) rather than clinical decision-making. This reflects both regulatory caution and practical opportunity—healthcare has significant administrative overhead that agents can address without requiring clinical validation.
Workforce: Hype vs Reality The hype machine surrounding AI agents reached new levels in April, even as enterprises struggled with basic questions about what AI agents actually are and how to deploy them.
The Reality Check ZDNet reported that 60% of AI agents work in IT departments . The finding suggests that despite the hype about agents transforming every business function, actual deployment is heavily concentrated in technical functions.
CIO.com explored how CIOs struggle with the definition of what makes a true AI agent. The terminology confusion—chatbots vs. copilots vs. agents vs. agentic AI—creates challenges for procurement and evaluation.
SiliconANGLE examined the long road to agentic AI , contrasting hype with enterprise reality.
HR Executive asked whether AI agent implementation has stalled and whether HR can propel it forward.
Actuia considered whether 2025 is the year of maturity for enterprise AI agents.
Cutting Through the Hype Salesforce introduced a 5-level framework for AI agents that cuts through the hype . The framework provides maturity levels to help enterprises distinguish between basic automation and true agentic systems.
UiPath AI agents blend with RPA amid industry hype and doubts , suggesting a more incremental evolution than revolutionary change.
Digiday profiled Salesforce’s transformation from CRM giant to “digital labor” provider , exploring how the company aims to “stand above the hype” with agentic AI.
Cautionary Tales A company apologized after its AI support agent invented a policy that caused user uproar. The incident highlights the risks of autonomous agents making statements or commitments beyond their authority—a governance challenge that enterprises must address.
Professors staffed a fake company entirely with AI agents in an experiment covered by Futurism and DIGIT . The results were mixed, showing both promise and limitation in current agent capabilities.
Who’s Interested? ZDNet analyzed the 4 types of people interested in AI agents and what businesses can learn from them.
Socradar asked whether AI agents are hype or reality .
NetworkWorld explored the distinction between AI agents vs. agentic AI and what enterprises actually want.
Market Signals: Funding and Startups Venture capital activity and startup moves provide signals about where the market is placing bets:
Artisan raises $25M with a provocative “stop hiring humans” pitch —though the startup is still hiring humans itself a16z backs UK startup Dex to scale an “AI talent agent” and recruitment matchmaker Model ML seeks to acquire AI agent companies according to its CEO A new agency is staffed with more AI agents than people and wants to keep it that way , according to Ad Age Make launched Make AI Agents to add real-time intelligence to no-code automation The funding pattern suggests investors are targeting specific horizontal use cases (recruitment, automation) rather than general-purpose agent platforms. The “stop hiring humans” framing generates attention, but the reality is more nuanced—companies are hiring humans to build and manage agents.
Developer Experience: Agents That Code Software development remains a key use case for AI agents:
Augment Code launched Augment Agent as an AI pair programmer that deeply understands codebases and learns as you work Microsoft Research published on Debug-gym exploring whether AI agents can lighten developers’ debugging load DevOps.com explored how AI agents are reshaping the developer experience Anthropic shared best practices for Claude Code agentic coding Augment Code published how to prompt your agent with 8 tips and best practices for using AI coding agents Coding agents benefit from clear evaluation criteria (does the code work?) and continuous feedback loops from integrated development environments. This makes them one of the more mature agent categories.
Industry Snapshot AI agents are spreading across industries:
Adobe is building AI agents for Photoshop and Premiere Pro , including an agent that can show you how to use Photoshop OneTrack launched AiOn as the first AI agent platform for autonomous logistics operations MineOS unveiled an AI agent to transform data privacy management SK Telecom touted AI agent ‘Aster’ as the future of telecom innovation Atlassian shared customer impressions of putting the Rovo AI agent to work Baidu rolled out new AI agent Xinxiang for Android KPMG reported that most companies are just test-driving AI agents Microsoft explored how AI and intelligent agents are transforming local government Real estate and travel industries explored agents for homebuyers and vacation planning Counterpoint Research analyzed how smartphone OEMs can stay competitive in the era of AI agents Computer Weekly explored how AI agents will reshape telecoms Looking Ahead: What April Means for Agents April 2025 was a foundational month for AI agents. The developments weren’t incremental—they were structural changes to how agents will be built, deployed, and managed in enterprises.
The protocol wars (A2A vs MCP vs ACP) will determine how agents interoperate. No standard has won yet, and fragmentation is likely to persist in the near term. Enterprises should prepare for multi-protocol environments.
The “agent boss” vision from Microsoft represents one possible future for work—humans managing teams of AI agents. But other vendors envision different models (human-AI collaboration, agents as assistants rather than subordinates). The org chart of the future is still being negotiated.
Security partnerships like CyberArk + Accenture address what could be a blocking issue for enterprise adoption. If agents can’t be secured, they won’t be deployed. The emergence of specialized agent security offerings suggests the market is taking this seriously.
Healthcare and commerce are leading use cases with clear ROI and relatively lower regulatory barriers. These industries provide a preview of how agents will transform workflows in other sectors.
The hype is real, but so are the challenges. CIOs struggle with definitions. Implementation has stalled in some places. Early failures like the policy-inventing agent show the risks. According to ZDnet, 60% of AI agents work in IT departments—suggesting transformation is concentrated, not universal.
The market is moving from “what are agents?” to “which platform and protocol win?” Expect the protocol war to intensify, security offerings to multiply, and enterprises to run more pilots. The next six months will determine whether 2025 is the year agents mature—or another hype cycle peak.

title: April's Agent War: Google's A2A Protocol, Microsoft's 'Agent Boss' Vision, and the Enterprise Rush to Agentic AI

This comprehensive review covers 285 articles published between March 1, 2025 and April 1, 2025, surveying a pivotal month for AI agents. OpenAI plans to charge $20,000 monthly for “PhD-level” AI agents while China’s Manus demonstrates fully autonomous capabilities. Every major tech company launched agent platforms, enterprises deployed agents at scale, and startups raised $93.8 million to solve critical infrastructure gaps.
The $20,000 Question OpenAI is reportedly planning to charge up to $20,000 per month for specialized AI agents designed to perform “PhD-level” research work, according to a report in The Information . The reported pricing strategy includes three tiers: $2,000 monthly for “high-income knowledge workers,” $10,000 for software development agents, and the $20,000 tier for research-intensive tasks requiring doctoral-level expertise.
The pricing is based on performance metrics from OpenAI’s o3 and o3-mini models, which use what the company calls “private chain of thought” reasoning. According to Ars Technica , o3 scored 87.5% on the ARC-AGI visual reasoning benchmark (comparable to the 85% human threshold), 96.7% on the 2024 American Invitational Mathematics Exam (missing just one question), and 87.7% on GPQA Diamond, which contains graduate-level biology, physics, and chemistry questions. On the Frontier Math benchmark by EpochAI, o3 solved 25.2% of problems while no other model has exceeded 2%.
The reported pricing represents a dramatic departure from current consumer AI costs. ChatGPT Plus remains $20 per month, Claude Pro costs $30 monthly, and even ChatGPT Pro’s $200/month subscription is tiny compared to the proposed enterprise fees. As xAI developer Hieu Pham noted in a widely-shared tweet: “most PhD students, including the brightest stars who can do way better work than any current LLMs—are not paid $20K / month.”
Behind the pricing strategy is significant financial pressure. OpenAI reportedly lost approximately $5 billion last year covering operational costs. At the same time, investor commitment remains strong: SoftBank has reportedly committed $3 billion to spend on OpenAI’s agent products this year alone.
Alongside the pricing news, OpenAI unveiled new tools for building AI agents, including a “reasoning” API that enables developers to build agents that can “think before they speak” using the company’s o3 models. The eWeek reported that these tools represent a “powerful suite” to simplify AI agent development.
However, skepticism about the “PhD-level” framing has emerged. As the Indian Express noted , “The hype around PhD-level AI comes with growing scepticism.” The models still struggle with confabulations—instances where they generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect information—which remains a critical concern for research applications where accuracy matters.
The Autonomous Agent Arrival While OpenAI focuses on premium pricing, a Chinese startup called Butterfly Effect has captured global attention with Manus, an AI agent described as the country’s first “fully autonomous” agent. According to Live Science , representatives claim Manus is “the world’s first general AI agent” designed to think, plan, and execute real-world tasks independently.
Unlike conventional AI tools that primarily assist users by providing recommendations or answering queries, Manus functions without human intervention . As The Economic Times explained , Manus “can come up with an itinerary for a trip to Japan, analyze stocks, and handle other complex tasks on its own.”
The emergence of Manus has drawn immediate comparisons to DeepSeek, another Chinese AI model that went viral earlier this year. As Axios reported , the new agent is “winning expert acclaim while stoking concern over another AI advance rooted in Chinese research and development.” Yicai Global claimed that Manus “is said to beat OpenAI’s Deep Research” in performance comparisons.
MIT Technology Review noted that researchers are actively testing Manus’s capabilities. The South China Morning Post reported that the startup’s founder believes Manus “transcends chatbots” in its ability to take independent action.
Manus added a mobile app and subscription plans in March, expanding access beyond web interfaces. Geeky Gadgets described how the agent is “redefining task automation and workflow management” through advanced automation, research, and coding capabilities.
The autonomous capabilities have also sparked discussion about how close we might be to artificial general intelligence (AGI). As Quartz noted , China now has a “completely autonomous” AI agent that operates differently from Western models. SiliconANGLE reported that the agent is “getting global attention for its autonomous smarts.”
Platform Wars: Big Tech’s Agent Offensive March marked a coordinated offensive from every major technology company, each launching agent platforms aimed at enterprise dominance.
Microsoft: 400,000 Agents Deployed Microsoft emerged as the early leader in the agent platform race. According to Cloud Wars , 160,000 customers have built 400,000 AI agents using the company’s Copilot platform. The scale demonstrates how quickly enterprises are moving beyond experimentation to deployment.
The company announced a range of specialized agents across different domains:
Security agents: Six new AI agents for security tasks, including phishing triage that can “handle routine phishing alerts and cyberattacks” and alert fatigue reduction that frees up human defenders Factory automation: New agents for manufacturing environments announced at Hannover Messe 2025 Sales agents: AI Accelerator for Sales and new sales agents to accelerate AI-first selling Research and data analysis: OpenAI-powered Copilot agents for workflow acceleration Microsoft also expanded partnerships: Adobe joined to empower marketers with AI agents in Microsoft 365 Copilot, while OneTrust launched an AI agent built with Microsoft Security Copilot.
ZDNET reported on two new “deep reasoning” AI agents that can speed up workflows. The company is positioning its agents as alternatives to Salesforce CRM systems.
Amazon: Browser Control in Nova Act Amazon entered the agent platform wars with Nova Act, an AI agent that can directly control web browsers to navigate websites and make purchases. According to The Verge , Amazon’s new agent “is designed to do your shopping.”
The browser-controlling capability represents a significant technical milestone. RetailWire reported that Nova Act “can take over a web browser and make purchases” on behalf of users. As PYMNTS noted , the agent can “shop and place orders” autonomously.
Beyond consumer applications, Amazon Web Services announced general availability of multi-agent collaboration on Bedrock, enabling multiple agents to work together on complex tasks. CNBC reported that the Nova launch “puts it up against rivals OpenAI, Anthropic.”
Salesforce: Agent Marketplace Salesforce pursued an app store-style strategy with AgentExchange, a marketplace for AI agent skills launched with 200+ initial partners . As Techzine Global reported , the marketplace is “specifically focused on skill-sharing” between agents.
The company also launched Agentforce 2dx, which enables AI agents to run in the background rather than requiring explicit user prompts. According to Techzine Global , the update sets “a new standard” as “AI agents become proactive.”
InfoWorld noted that the update aims to simplify AI agent development and deployment. Salesforce DevOps reported that AgentExchange is designed to “drive adoption of role-based AI agents.”
In healthcare, Salesforce released pre-built AI agents to tackle “time-consuming healthcare tasks.”
Oracle: No-Code Agent Studio Oracle introduced AI Agent Studio, a no-code tool for creating AI agents across its Fusion application suite. According to Oracle’s announcement , the studio is “available at no additional cost” and delivers “easy-to-use tools, including advanced testing, robust validation, and built-in security.”
ZDNET reported that the new tool is an “impressive next step for Oracle’s AI strategy.” Capacity Global noted that the studio enables businesses to “build custom AI agents.”
Oracle announced AI agents for financial crime detection, adding a “broad class of AI agents and agentic workflows” to its Investigation Hub Cloud Service. SiliconANGLE reported that customers can “create and modify AI agents across” the Fusion suite.
The company also announced general availability of its OCI Generative AI Agents Platform. As Techzine Global noted , Oracle is positioning Agent Studio for Fusion Cloud Applications.
ServiceNow: Pre-Built Agent Library ServiceNow took a vertical-specific approach with its Yokohama platform release, which adds to “thousands of AI agents across CRM, HR, IT, and more,” according to the Business Wire announcement .
The company introduced AI agents built for the telecom industry . These agents, built with NVIDIA AI Enterprise software and DGX Cloud, are designed to “drive productivity across the entire service lifecycle.”
Diginomica reported that Yokohama is “unleashing pre-configured AI agents, everywhere.” CX Today noted that ServiceNow is “going big on industry-specific innovation” with new AI agents and the Quality 360 acquisition.
Constellation Research reported that the Yokohama release “ups AI agent game” with ServiceNow Studio, an AI-powered workspace for no-code, low-code, and pro-code agent development. Techzine Global noted that ServiceNow is introducing “new AI agents for telecoms.”
Other Platform Players Several other companies announced agent platforms:
PwC launched an AI agent operating system to “revolutionize AI workflows for enterprises” Workato launched its enterprise AI agent platform and acquired AI customer support vendor DeepConverse EY announced the EY.ai Agentic Platform , created with NVIDIA AI, for tax, risk, and finance domains NVIDIA launched a family of open reasoning AI models for building agentic AI platforms Kore.ai announced an agent platform for “building, deploying, and orchestrating agentic applications” WSO2 expanded AI agent capabilities with platform-wide AI-native updates Accenture debuted an AI agent builder within its AI Refinery platform Deloitte unveiled Zora AI , described as “agentic AI for tomorrow’s workforce” Adobe launched the Adobe Experience Platform Agent Orchestrator for businesses to activate AI agents The Browser Pattern: Agents That Navigate the Web A clear pattern emerged in March: browser-controlling agents as a primary interface for AI automation.
Browser Use raised $17 million in a funding round to help AI agents navigate websites. As TechCrunch explained , the startup is “making it easier for AI ‘agents’ to navigate websites.” SiliconANGLE reported that the funding will help “steer AI agents through the internet.”
Opera introduced “Browser Operator,” a native AI agent integrated directly into the browser to perform tasks for users. The screenshot from the announcement shows the agent designed to handle web-based workflows without leaving the browser.
Amazon’s Nova Act represents the most ambitious browser-controlling agent to date, with the ability to navigate websites and make purchases directly. The capability matters because it allows agents to interact with existing web infrastructure without requiring API integrations.
However, browser control also creates security concerns. Arcade.dev raised $12 million in seed funding specifically “to solve the biggest security problem with AI Agents.” As the company noted, it is “the first company to help AI agents securely take real-world actions on behalf of a user.”
Security Double-Edged: Agents as Defender and Threat Agents as Defenders Microsoft led the charge on using AI agents for security, announcing six specialized security agents for Security Copilot . According to The Verge , the agents will “help overwhelmed humans” by handling routine security tasks.
Help Net Security reported that the new AI agents “take on phishing, patching, alert fatigue.” The phishing triage agent specifically can “handle routine phishing alerts and cyberattacks, freeing up human defenders.”
SailPoint unveiled Harbor Pilot, a set of AI-powered agents for identity security . The agents are designed to “help identity teams work smarter, respond faster and secure their organizations more efficiently.”
Alpha Vision announced it will showcase AI agent-powered security solutions at ISC West 2025, demonstrating how agents can enhance physical security.
Oracle brought AI agents to financial crime detection , adding agents and agentic workflows to its Investigation Hub Cloud Service.
Agents as Attackers But security researchers also demonstrated how AI agents can be used maliciously. SC Media reported that OpenAI’s Operator AI agent “can be used in phishing attacks.” Researchers showed that the same browser-controlling capabilities that make agents useful for legitimate tasks also enable them to conduct autonomous phishing attacks .
The dual-use nature of agent capabilities creates a security dilemma. As Arcade.dev noted in its funding announcement, securely enabling AI agents to “take real-world actions on behalf of a user” is one of the most critical challenges facing the industry.
Vertical Agents: Healthcare, Finance, and Beyond Healthcare Salesforce released pre-built AI agents specifically designed to “tackle time-consuming healthcare tasks.” The agents target administrative workflows that consume provider time.
Wipro announced AI agent solutions for healthcare transformation , powered by Salesforce’s Agentforce platform.
Nature published a paper on “coordinated AI agents for advancing healthcare,” exploring how multi-agent systems can improve medical workflows.
Financial Services Auquan launched an industry-first AI agent purpose-built for risk monitoring in financial services. As Corporate Compliance Insights noted , Auquan launched an “agentic AI risk agent for FinServ.”
Oscilar announced how it is transforming risk decisioning with AI agents, targeting financial risk assessment workflows.
Oracle expanded its financial crime detection agents , adding a broad class of AI agents to its Investigation Hub Cloud Service.
Other Industries Telecommunications: ServiceNow introduced AI agents built for the telecom industry , designed to drive productivity across the entire service lifecycle.
Manufacturing: Microsoft launched new AI agents for factory automation at Hannover Messe 2025. Ford is using agents with NVIDIA for distributed inference with collaborative AI agents.
Real Estate: An AI agent claiming to be the “world’s first AI real estate agent” has generated $100M in sales . As The Express Tribune reported , the agent generated $100M in sales for Portugal real estate.
Retail: A Salesforce report found that 75% of retailers say AI agents will be “essential by 2026.” Amazon’s Nova Act directly targets retail shopping workflows.
Infrastructure Funding: Building the Agent Stack Startup funding in March reveals where the agent ecosystem needs work. Infrastructure startups raised $93.8 million across several categories:
Browser Control & Security Browser Use: Raised $17M for web navigation infrastructure Arcade.dev: Raised $12M to solve agent security problems Compliance & Payments Norm Ai: Raised $48M for compliance automation agents Paid: Raised $10.8M to “scale financial infrastructure for AI agents” Specialized Infrastructure Tiga.ai: Raised $2M to launch an AI agent for custom buying signals Nunu.ai: Secured $6M to scale AI agents for game QA testing Agent Monetization Manny Medina (former Outreach CEO) launched a new startup tackling AI agent monetization. As TechCrunch noted , the startup “helps AI agents get paid.” Platform Plays Several consulting firms and platforms launched agent offerings:
Powered_by launched the “world’s first AI agency for SMBs” to help small businesses deploy agents Tarka raised funding to arm go-to-market teams with AI agents Oracle announced general availability of its OCI Generative AI Agents Platform Adobe launched Adobe Experience Platform Agent Orchestrator Reality Check: Why Agents Struggle Despite the platform launches and funding, critical voices reminded the industry that significant challenges remain.
A widely-cited article titled “Why AI Agents Suck So Bad” detailed frustrating experiences with support agents, highlighting “limitations of current RAG-based AI systems in handling complex customer” issues.
More than half of companies have already deployed autonomous AI agents, according to a study by PagerDuty covered by Quartz. But adoption doesn’t equal satisfaction—implementation challenges abound.
CIO reported that IT leaders are “bracing for the AI agent management challenge.” As organizations deploy more agents, managing them becomes increasingly complex.
Skepticism about “PhD-level” marketing claims continues. As the Indian Express noted , “The hype around PhD-level AI comes with growing scepticism.”
Hidden risks in agent adoption are emerging, including concerns about data silos impacting agent performance. Enterprises face real management complexity as agent deployments scale.
What This Month Means March 2025 was when AI agents graduated from research project to product. The evidence is across several dimensions:
Pricing as value signal: OpenAI’s reported $20,000 monthly pricing suggests the company believes these systems can deliver substantial enterprise value—even if the “PhD-level” framing remains marketing rhetoric.
Autonomous capabilities are here: China’s Manus demonstrated what fully autonomous agents can do, planning complex tasks without human intervention and drawing comparisons to DeepSeek’s viral impact.
Platform ubiquity: Every major tech company—Microsoft, Amazon, Salesforce, Oracle, ServiceNow—now offers an agent platform. The land grab for enterprise mindshare is underway.
Infrastructure being built: Startup funding of $93.8 million in a single month shows where the ecosystem needs work: browser control, security, payments, compliance, and monitoring.
Enterprise adoption accelerating: Microsoft’s 400,000 agents built by 160,000 customers, the PagerDuty study finding more than half of companies using autonomous agents, and industry-specific deployments all point to real adoption.
But we’re still early. Reliability issues persist, management complexity is real, and the gap between marketing claims and actual capabilities—especially around “PhD-level” performance—remains significant.
The next 6-12 months will be about deployment at scale. Which platforms actually deliver value? Which use cases prove durable? The agent wars have begun, but the winner is far from determined.

title: The AI Agent Wars: $20,000 Agents, Autonomous Systems, and Enterprise Platforms Battle for Supremacy

This comprehensive review covers 10 articles published during March 2025, surveying the latest developments in materials discovery. AI-driven autonomous labs are exploring vast chemical spaces at unprecedented scale, while researchers reported breakthrough materials from quantum dots to ultra-bright fluorescents. The trend is attracting top AI talent, with an OpenAI vice president departing to launch an AI-powered materials science startup.
The Acceleration Engine: AI and Automation in Materials Discovery The most significant trend this month is the maturation of AI-driven autonomous laboratories that can systematically explore combinatorial spaces far beyond human capacity.
Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Chicago reported on Polybot , an AI-driven autonomous laboratory that explored nearly a million possible processing combinations for electronic polymer thin films. The system uses robotics and AI to autonomously run experiments, optimizing material properties like conductivity and coating defects. The research team has produced recipes for large-scale production and will share the collected data openly with the scientific community.
In parallel validation work, researchers from the University of Michigan and Samsung Advanced Institute of Technology demonstrated a new precursor selection method for inorganic materials synthesis. Using the Samsung ASTRAL robotic lab , they synthesized 35 target materials across 224 reactions , working with 27 elements and 28 unique precursors. The new approach achieved higher purity for 32 of the 35 materials . As the Department of Energy noted, this combination of improved precursor selection and robotic synthesis can “greatly accelerate materials discovery” and “reduce bottlenecks in manufacturing” known and predicted materials.
These demonstrations establish a clear pattern: AI-guided autonomous systems can now systematically explore chemical and materials spaces that would be impractical for manual experimentation, accelerating the path from prediction to validated material.
Performance Breakthroughs: New Materials with Quantified Gains The acceleration in discovery tools is translating into materials with quantified performance improvements across applications.
Next-Generation Displays Curtin University researchers, in collaboration with Shanghai University, Jilin University, the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Fudan University, and TCL Research, have developed non-toxic blue quantum dot LEDs that achieve 24.7% efficiency with a 30,000-hour operational lifetime . The ZnSeTeS quantum dots avoid heavy metals like cadmium, addressing a key environmental concern for display technology. This efficiency-lifetime combination for blue QLEDs could enable brighter, eco-friendly displays for TVs, smartphones, and VR headsets. The work was published in Nature.
Medical Imaging Indiana University chemists reported ultra-bright fluorescent materials called SMILES that reach 30,000 brightness units - five times brighter than the team’s 2020 report. The materials achieve brightness through “supra-dancing” molecular behavior, where strategically placed atoms enable intense light emission. Potential applications include tumor labeling for cancer surgery and biological imaging. The work appears in Nature Chemistry.
Neural Interfaces Rice University researchers, collaborating with Stanford University and the University of Cambridge, discovered that thermal processing of PEDOT:PSS beyond typical thresholds triples electrical conductivity while eliminating the need for chemical crosslinkers . The crosslinker removal addresses a potential source of toxicity, and the processed material maintains stability in water for 20 days with consistent performance. This could accelerate development of neural implants, biosensors, and neuromorphic computing devices.
Material Breakthrough Metric Application Source ZnSeTeS Quantum Dots 24.7% efficiency , 30,000-hour lifetime Eco-friendly displays Curtin University SMILES Fluorescents 30,000 brightness units Medical diagnostics Indiana University PEDOT:PSS (thermally processed) 3x conductivity , no crosslinker Neural implants Rice University The Role of Serendipity: Accidental Findings That Advance Science Alongside systematic AI-driven approaches, serendipitous discoveries continue to advance materials science.
Heavy Element Chemistry A research team at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory has discovered “berkelocene” , the first organometallic molecule containing berkelium . Working with just 0.3 milligrams of berkelium-249 - the element was first discovered at Berkeley Lab in 1949 - the team found that berkelium exhibits an unexpected +4 oxidation state in its organometallic form. This provides new insights into later actinide behavior, which is crucial for models related to nuclear waste storage and remediation. The work was published in Science.
Pattern Formation UCLA researchers discovered that spiral patterns spontaneously form on germanium surfaces when chemical reactions couple with mechanical stress. The spirals emerge from a reaction-diffusion-convection process that creates instabilities at the reaction front. The researchers developed a theoretical framework explaining the pattern formation, offering a model for understanding similar processes in biological systems. The work appears in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
These discoveries underscore that while AI acceleration expands the scope of exploration, human observation and the ability to recognize unexpected phenomena remain essential to scientific discovery.
Quantum Sensing for Materials Characterization A new characterization technique from Oak Ridge National Laboratory uses a nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond as both a quantum bit and a sensor to measure high-speed magnetic fluctuations in materials. The scanning NV center microscope detects spin fluctuations near phase transitions in magnetic thin films at room temperature . Led by Ben Lawrie and Yueh-Chun Wu , the work provides a nanoscale method for probing quantum materials, with potential applications in data storage, sensing, and quantum computing. The research was published in Nano Letters.
Industry Signal: AI Talent Migrates to Materials Science The field is attracting serious talent and investment. Liam Fedus, vice president of research for post-training at OpenAI , has departed to launch an AI-powered materials science startup . OpenAI has confirmed it will invest in and collaborate with the new venture. Fedus joined OpenAI in 2022 and was promoted to vice president in 2024.
His departure reflects a broader trend: top AI researchers are moving to apply machine learning to scientific discovery. Google DeepMind introduced the GNoME materials discovery system in 2023, while Microsoft rolled out MatterGen and MatterSim for materials generation and simulation. The migration of senior AI talent to materials science signals market validation for AI-accelerated discovery approaches.
Additional Developments The University of Liverpool’s Materials Innovation Factory is leveraging digital tools to shorten materials innovation timelines . A recent project led by Matt Reed applied materials characterization techniques to dinosaur fossil study, demonstrating how analytical tools cross disciplines. This interdisciplinary approach shows how materials science methods contribute to fields beyond traditional materials applications.
title: AI Accelerates Materials Discovery as Breakthrough Materials Emerge

March brought conflicting narratives in quantum computing: D-Wave claimed the first practical quantum supremacy demonstration, China unveiled a processor reportedly quadrillions of times faster than supercomputers, and Microsoft faced fierce criticism over its topological qubit breakthrough. Meanwhile, the industry poured billions into scaling hardware, with PsiQuantum raising $750 million and NVIDIA opening a dedicated quantum research center.
This comprehensive review covers 45 articles published in March 2025, surveying the latest developments in quantum computing.
The Skeptical Breakthrough In February, Microsoft unveiled Majorana 1, a quantum chip with a Topological Core architecture that theoretically enables stable and scalable qubits using topoconductors—materials that host exotic Majorana particles first theorized in 1937. The chip contains 8 topological qubits, and Microsoft says this architecture paves the way for million-qubit machines capable of solving complex problems within years.
But physicists aren’t buying it. A Nature report published March 18 documents widespread skepticism, with researchers saying the evidence is insufficient to support the claims. Henry Legg, a physicist at the University of St. Andrews, challenged the validity of a key test underlying Microsoft’s claims. Sergey Frolov, a professor at the University of Pittsburgh, called the project “unreliable” and cited a lack of established physics in Microsoft’s work.
Critics note this isn’t the first time Microsoft’s Majorana research has faced scrutiny—the company retracted a 2018 paper claiming detection of Majorana particles. The controversy echoes the field’s broader reproducibility crisis: extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and Microsoft’s latest work has not convinced many experts.
At the American Physical Society’s Global Physics Summit on March 19, Chetan Nayak, a Microsoft researcher, presented new data defending the work. But hundreds of physicists attending the talk remained unconvinced, with some arguing the data looks like noise and the methods are flawed. Microsoft stands by its research and continues development, but the episode underscores the high standards required for breakthrough claims in quantum computing.
Three Supremacy Claims, Different Approaches While Microsoft’s claims faced skepticism, three other groups announced quantum performance claims—each using different technologies, different benchmarks, and different levels of peer review.
D-Wave: First Practical Supremacy? D-Wave published peer-reviewed results in Science showing its Advantage2 annealing quantum computer solved a materials simulation problem (a spin glass system) in minutes that would take the Frontier supercomputer approximately 1 million years to complete. This wasn’t a random benchmark—it was a practical scientific problem that researchers actually care about.
The study, led by researchers including Andrew King from D-Wave and Daniel Lidar from the University of Southern California, represents the first peer-reviewed demonstration of what the authors call “practical quantum supremacy”—solving a problem of practical significance faster than any classical computer could. The work built on D-Wave’s previous research using a reverse annealing protocol that allows the system to refine solutions iteratively.
Jared Rovny, a physicist at D-Wave, noted that the performance gap is so large that classical computers would need to improve by many orders of magnitude to compete. Annealing quantum computers like D-Wave’s are fundamentally different from gate-based systems—they excel at optimization problems rather than general-purpose computation, which explains why this result came on a practical materials science problem rather than an abstract benchmark.
China’s Zuchongzhi-3: Speedup on Random Circuits Chinese researchers from the University of Science and Technology of China (USTC) unveiled Zuchongzhi 3.0, a 105-qubit superconducting processor that reportedly performs random circuit sampling (RCS)—a standard quantum benchmark—2 million billion times faster than the Frontier supercomputer. The results were published as a cover article in Physical Review Letters.
The processor achieved:
99.90% parallel single-qubit gate fidelity 99.62% parallel two-qubit gate fidelity 72 microsecond coherence times 182 couplers connecting the qubits in a 2D grid architecture On the RCS benchmark with 83 qubits and 32 circuit layers, Zuchongzhi 3.0 completed the task in a few hundred seconds. The researchers estimate it would take Frontier approximately 6.4 billion years to simulate the same computation—a speedup factor of roughly \(2 \times 10^{15}\), or 15 orders of magnitude.
However, experts note this benchmark favors quantum methods by design. RCS doesn’t solve a practical problem—it’s designed to be hard for classical computers. Additionally, classical algorithms have improved dramatically since Google’s 2019 supremacy claim, with GPU-based simulations completing Google’s original task in 14 seconds. The Zuchongzhi results push the frontier further, but the practical applications remain limited.
Pan Jianwei, Zhu Xiaobo, and Chengzhi Peng led the USTC team, which has previously demonstrated quantum supremacy with both the Jiuzhang photonic systems and earlier Zuchongzhi superconducting processors.
Certified Randomness: A Provably Quantum Task A collaboration between Quantinuum, the University of Texas at Austin, JPMorganChase, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and Argonne National Laboratory achieved something truly new: certified randomness that is provably impossible for classical computers to generate.
Using a 56-qubit Quantinuum H2 trapped-ion quantum computer, the team applied a protocol first proposed by Scott Aaronson in 2018 to generate random numbers that were then mathematically verified by classical supercomputers with a combined 1.1 exaflops of sustained performance. The team certified 71,313 bits of entropy—randomness that can be mathematically proven to be genuinely unpredictable.
The research, published in Nature on March 26, represents a practical quantum application with real-world utility. Certified randomness is crucial for:
Cryptography: Generating unguessable encryption keys Fairness: Ensuring truly random selections in lotteries and elections Privacy: Creating random numbers that cannot be predicted or manipulated Unlike the other supremacy claims, certified randomness isn’t about speed—it’s about capability. Classical computers provably cannot generate this type of mathematically verifiable randomness, making it a fundamental demonstration of quantum advantage.
Rajeeb Hazra, CEO of Quantinuum, called the milestone “a practical application of quantum computing that is beyond the reach of classical systems.”
Company Technology Benchmark Speedup Peer Review D-Wave Annealing (Advantage2) Spin glass simulation Minutes vs. 1M years Yes (Science) China (USTC) Superconducting (105 qubits) Random circuit sampling \(2 \times 10^{15}\)x faster Pending (PRL) Quantinuum + partners Trapped-ion (56 qubits) Certified randomness Classically impossible Yes (Nature) Hardware Advances: Scaling and Error Correction Beyond the headline-grabbing supremacy claims, March brought significant advances in quantum hardware—particularly in error correction, the bottleneck that determines whether large-scale quantum computing becomes practical.
Error Correction Breakthroughs Fujitsu, QuTech, and TU Delft set a new world record by achieving quantum gate error rates below 0.1% using a two-qubit system built on diamond spin qubits. Some gates achieved error rates as low as 0.001%. The researchers used ultrapure synthetic diamonds from Element Six and designed quantum gates to decouple qubits from environmental noise.
This milestone is significant because error correction requires physical qubits with error rates low enough that logical qubits can be constructed with reasonable overhead. The diamond spin qubits operate at 10 Kelvin, warmer than the millikelvin temperatures required by superconducting qubits, and the team plans to scale up by adding more nuclear spins and developing optical interconnects for networking.
In late February, Amazon Web Services (AWS) unveiled Ocelot, its first prototype quantum computing chip focused on error correction. Ocelot uses novel “bosonic cat qubits”—a type of qubit encoded in harmonic oscillator states that are naturally resistant to bit-flip errors. The chip uses a one-dimensional repetition code that AWS claims reduces error correction overhead by up to 90% compared to traditional surface codes.
The numbers are striking:
Traditional approach: ~49 physical qubits needed for one logical qubit Ocelot approach: 9 physical qubits needed (5 data qubits, 4 ancilla qubits) Ocelot’s cat qubits maintain bit-flip stability for 1 second—orders of magnitude longer than the 50-100 microsecond coherence times of traditional transmon qubits. The phase-flip time is 20 microseconds, which the system corrects through its repetition code architecture. This hardware-efficient approach could dramatically accelerate progress toward fault-tolerant quantum systems.
Architecture Innovations MIT researchers developed a novel quantum interconnect that enables all-to-all communication between superconducting quantum processors. The team demonstrated remote entanglement between two processors using a superconducting waveguide, achieving over 60% photon absorption efficiency. This interconnect paves the way for scalable quantum networks and distributed quantum computing by allowing modules to communicate directly without complex routing architectures.
NTT Corporation and collaborators proposed a new load-store architecture for fault-tolerant quantum computing that separates memory and processor, similar to classical computer architecture. This approach achieves:
Up to 100% asymptotic memory efficiency ~90% practical memory efficiency Only a ~3% increase in computation time compared to ideal systems This represents a significant improvement over conventional quantum computers, which achieve only 44-67% memory efficiency. The architecture enables more efficient use of quantum hardware and improves program portability across different quantum systems.
Researchers are also exploring alternatives to traditional qubits. Nature highlighted the emerging field of “qudits”—quantum information units that can exist in three or more simultaneous states (compared to qubits’ two states). Qudits offer increased information density and could reduce the number of quantum elements needed for certain computations.
Room-Temperature and Modular Systems Xanadu launched Aurora, the world’s first modular, room-temperature photonic quantum computer. The system uses:
35 interconnected photonic chips 8 miles (13 kilometers) of fiber optic cables Room-temperature operation—no cryogenic cooling required Photonic quantum computing uses particles of light rather than matter-based qubits, enabling room-temperature operation and fiber-optic networking. Xanadu’s modular approach tackles scalability and error correction by allowing the system to be expanded through additional modules. The Nature-published architecture could enable practical quantum data centers and new applications in molecular simulation and cryptography.
Company Innovation Key Metric Significance Fujitsu/QuTech/TU Delft Diamond spin qubits 0.1% error rate Error correction milestone Amazon (AWS) Ocelot chip with cat qubits 90% overhead reduction Fewer physical qubits needed Xanadu Aurora modular system Room-temperature operation No cryogenic cooling MIT Quantum interconnect All-to-all communication Scalable architecture Ecosystem Development: OS, Networking, and AI Integration As hardware advances, the quantum ecosystem is maturing with new operating systems, networking capabilities, and integration with classical AI computing.
Quantum Operating Systems OQTOPUS (Open Quantum Toolchain for Operators and Users), an open-source quantum computer operating system, launched on GitHub from a consortium led by Osaka University, Fujitsu, SEC, and TIS. The OS covers the full stack from quantum computer setup to operation, lowering the barrier to deploying quantum computers via the cloud. Fujitsu plans to make OQTOPUS available to research partners in the second half of 2025.
Separately, researchers published QNodeOS in Nature—a quantum network operating system that enables platform-independent execution of quantum network applications in high-level software. The system was demonstrated on quantum network nodes based on:
Nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond (2 nodes) Trapped-ion systems (1 node with a single 40Ca+ atom) QNodeOS allows multitasking and efficient hardware use, abstracting underlying physical complexities so users can execute applications without detailed knowledge of the specific quantum systems. This work, described as a “huge practical step forward” in a Nature commentary , provides a critical abstraction layer for the emerging quantum internet.
AI + Quantum NVIDIA announced the NVIDIA Accelerated Quantum Research Center (NVAQC) in Boston to integrate AI supercomputing with quantum computing. The center will deploy 576 Blackwell GPUs and use Quantum-2 InfiniBand networking to tackle challenges like qubit noise and error correction. Partners include Quantinuum, Quantum Machines, QuEra Computing, Harvard University, and MIT.
Interestingly, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang recently estimated that practical quantum computers are likely 20 years away, noting a gap of 5-6 orders of magnitude in qubit count needed for useful systems. Yet NVIDIA is investing now to develop the hybrid quantum-classical systems that will bridge that gap.
On the theoretical side, Google Quantum AI researchers published work showing quantum algorithms could learn “periodic neuron” neural networks exponentially faster than classical methods. The proposed approach uses a modified quantum Fourier transform within a Quantum Statistical Query learning model to find hidden patterns in data. This work is purely theoretical—it doesn’t demonstrate a practical speedup on current hardware—but identifies a specific problem class where quantum computers might offer provable advantages.
Industry-Academia Partnerships In Germany, Fraunhofer IAO, Fraunhofer IPA, and the University of Stuttgart established “flaQship”, a cross-institute lab to pool research expertise in applied quantum computing. The lab focuses on quantum machine learning, material simulation, and error correction, aiming to create value for companies and society. The collaboration will organize the ML4QT symposium in July 2025 to advance quantum technology through machine learning.
Money and Momentum: The Investment Surge March revealed the massive capital flowing into quantum computing, with venture funding setting records and governments making strategic bets.
Mega-Rounds PsiQuantum is raising at least $750 million at a $6 billion valuation to fund its development of million-qubit, fault-tolerant photonic quantum computers. The company is leveraging traditional chip manufacturing at GlobalFoundries and has secured major public partnerships:
$500 million from the State of Illinois, Cook County, and Chicago for a U.S. quantum computer project $617 million (AUD $940 million) from Australian governments for a Brisbane computer PsiQuantum targets 2029 to deliver its first commercial system, positioning it as a competitor to tech giants pursuing different qubit technologies.
China launched a massive $138 billion government-backed venture fund to invest in emerging technologies including quantum computing, AI, and semiconductors. The fund aims to commercialize research and enhance technological self-reliance, dwarfing Western initiatives:
U.S. National Quantum Initiative: $1.2 billion over five years (2018), with $2.7 billion proposed for reauthorization Europe’s Quantum Flagship: ~$1.1 billion over 10 years IonQ raised $372.6 million through a share sale, bringing its total cash balance to over $700 million. The funding follows strategic moves including acquiring a majority stake in quantum networking provider ID Quantique and forming a partnership with SK Telecom. IonQ also commissioned a quantum networking system at the U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory as part of over $94.4 million in contracts.
Growth Funding Smaller but strategically important rounds included:
QuamCore (Israel): $9 million seed funding for architecture enabling 1 million superconducting qubits in a single cryostat by reducing cabling by a factor of 1,000 QuantWare (Netherlands): 20 million Series A for VIO technology to scale quantum processors to 1 million+ qubits; also launched pre-orders for “Contralto-A” QPU, nearly twice as large as competing solutions Singapore: $18.3 million SGD for HQCC 1.0, a national initiative to integrate quantum and high-performance computing Australia: $15 million government investment in QuintessenceLabs for quantum cybersecurity Iceberg Quantum: $2 million pre-seed and partnership with PsiQuantum to apply quantum LDPC codes for error correction overhead reduction The broader trend is clear: 2024 set a new venture funding record for quantum computing startups at $1.9 billion, up 138% from 2023’s $789 million, according to Crunchbase data . Momentum continues into 2025 with massive individual rounds including QuEra Computing’s $230 million and Quantum Machines’ $170 million.
Not everyone is keeping pace. A report in The Times warns the UK risks falling behind due to government spending delays, despite strong research from institutions like Oxford University and startups like Oxford Ionics (which has raised 37 million and employs 80 engineers). Competitors including the U.S. and Germany are moving faster with larger contracts.
What March Really Means Stepping back from individual news items, three patterns emerge from March’s developments:
First, quantum supremacy claims are diversifying. D-Wave demonstrated advantage on a practical materials simulation problem using annealing. China’s Zuchongzhi-3 showed massive speedup on random circuit sampling. Quantinuum and partners proved certified randomness is classically impossible. These aren’t competing claims on a single benchmark—they’re demonstrations of different quantum approaches excelling at different tasks. The field isn’t a single race anymore; it’s branching into multiple technological paths.
Second, skepticism is healthy. The controversy around Microsoft’s Majorana 1 chip shows the field is maturing and demanding rigorous evidence. After past retractions and exaggerated claims, physicists are rightfully insisting on extraordinary evidence for extraordinary breakthroughs. This skepticism doesn’t slow progress—it strengthens it by ensuring resources flow to reproducible, verifiable advances.
Third, the real story is money. $1.9 billion in 2024 VC funding (up 138%), massive government investments like China’s $138 billion fund, and huge bets on specific approaches like PsiQuantum’s $750 million for photonics and D-Wave’s annealing systems. The debate has shifted from “will quantum work?” to “which approach will scale?”
March didn’t resolve the fundamental questions in quantum computing. Error correction remains challenging, practical applications are still emerging, and timelines for fault-tolerant systems span years to decades. But the month clarified the stakes: companies and countries are placing substantial bets on different technological approaches, hardware is making measurable progress on error correction and scaling, and the ecosystem is developing the software and infrastructure needed to make quantum computers usable.
The race isn’t about a single breakthrough anymore—it’s about which combination of qubit technology, error correction approach, and ecosystem development reaches practical scale first. March brought progress on all three fronts.
title: Quantum Computing in March: Supremacy Claims, Skepticism, and the Race to Scale

This comprehensive review covers 3 articles published between February 1 and February 26, 2025, surveying how artificial intelligence is transforming materials science. Research reviews demonstrate accelerated discovery in MXenes and perovskites, while industry data reveals 74% of chemical companies are now deploying AI in R&D.
Research Spotlight: Computational Methods Accelerate Discovery Two review articles published this month document how computational methods are accelerating materials discovery, demonstrating a consistent pattern: artificial intelligence and first-principles calculations work together to guide experimental work.
MXenes: Computational Prediction Guides Experiment MXenes , a family of 2D transition metal carbides and nitrides discovered in 2011, have seen interest grow at 34% annually according to a review in npj Computational Materials . This rapid growth creates a challenge: researchers must navigate an exponentially expanding design space to identify promising compositions for specific applications.
The review highlights how density functional theory (DFT) and machine learning are being used together to predict MXene properties before synthesis. DFT calculations allow researchers to explore electronic structure, surface chemistry, and mechanical properties across the MXene family. Various functionals appear in the literature, including PBE, TPSS, M06, B3LYP, PBE0, HSE06, and others from Perdew’s “Jacob’s ladder” of density functional approximations.
Machine learning complements these first-principles calculations by learning patterns from computed datasets, enabling faster prediction of properties for new MXene compositions. This computational guidance helps narrow the vast design space, directing experimental synthesis toward the most promising candidates. The review notes that despite progress, challenges remain in transitioning MXenes from laboratory demonstrations to practical applications.
Perovskites: Automation Drives Efficiency Gains Perovskite photovoltaics present a similar story of computational acceleration. Since their emergence in 2009, perovskite solar cells have seen power conversion efficiency rise from 3.8% to over 26%, according to a review in InfoMat . This rapid improvement has been driven partly by machine learning and automation.
The review, authored by researchers from Forschungszentrum Jülich, Helmholtz-Institute Erlangen-Nürnberg (HI ERN), and the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China (UESTC), describes how Autonomous Material and Device Acceleration Platforms (AMADAP) enable high-throughput experimentation. These automated systems can prepare samples, test devices, and feed results back into machine learning models that suggest the next experiment.
Materials with the \(ABX_3\) perovskite structure present optimization challenges due to the vast parameter space of compositions, processing conditions, and device architectures. ML-driven automation addresses this by exploring more combinations faster than manual methods allow. The review notes various deposition techniques being automated, including spin-coating, doctor-blading, and spray-coating.
Both MXenes and perovskites demonstrate the same underlying pattern: computational methods don’t replace experimentation, but they make it more efficient by predicting what to try next.
Industry Adoption: AI Moves from Lab to Production The computational methods documented in academic research are now being deployed at scale across the chemicals industry. According to an analysis by Elsevier , 74% of chemical companies have begun implementing AI in their R&D processes. This finding comes from an IBM survey of 400 chemicals executives, 80% of whom said AI will be important to their business in the next three years.
The article highlights a concrete example from Dow Polyurethane, where AI has transformed foam formulation development. Previously, developing new flexible foam formulations took experts 4 to 6 months of iterative testing. With AI, this process now takes seconds. Rather than replacing the experts, the AI augments their capabilities, allowing them to explore more options and reach optimal formulations faster.
McKinsey & Company estimates that generative AI could create $140 billion in value across the energy and materials sector by accelerating the identification of new molecules and formulations. This potential is driving rapid adoption, but the article emphasizes that success depends on a critical foundation: data.
**FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable)] are essential for effective AI deployment. Elsevier works with companies like Johnson Matthey to build “data scaffolding” through enrichment, knowledge graphs, and semantic search. SciBite, an Elsevier company, provides semantic technology to structure chemical and biological data for AI applications.
The article also mentions broader AI initiatives in the industry, including Microsoft and Surveily using AI for predictive maintenance and safety monitoring in chemical plants. These applications extend beyond R&D into operations, showing AI’s potential to improve safety and sustainability alongside accelerating innovation.
The Pattern: Integration, Not Replacement The three articles from February reveal a consistent theme: AI is integrating into materials science and chemical engineering as an augmentation tool, not a replacement for expertise. In academic research, DFT calculations guide MXene synthesis exploration, and ML-driven automation accelerates perovskite efficiency improvements. In industry, AI formulations tools reduce development time from months to seconds, but experts remain in the loop.
The common thread across all these developments is the integration of computational methods with domain knowledge. DFT + ML for MXenes, automation + ML for perovskites, and AI + expert formulation guidance at Dow all follow the same pattern: the technology augments, accelerates, and extends what human researchers can achieve.
Success depends on foundations that aren’t glamorous but are essential: high-quality computational data for training ML models, FAIR-compliant data infrastructure in industry, and experimental validation of computational predictions. As the survey data shows, the chemicals industry has moved beyond asking whether AI is useful to asking how to deploy it effectively. The research literature suggests materials science is following the same trajectory.
title: AI Accelerates Materials Discovery: From Lab to Industry
